questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 9 years attends his annual review. An early-morning urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is 5.2 mg/mmol; eGFR is 81 mL/min/1.73m².
questions.ask: Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.explanation: A raised uACR (above 2.5 mg/mmol in men) can be transient, for example after exercise, fever or a UTI. Kidney Health Australia and the RACGP advise confirming albuminuria with 2 of 3 raised samples within 3 months before diagnosing diabetic kidney disease. Once it is confirmed, an ACE inhibitor or ARB is titrated and an SGLT2 inhibitor is favoured.
why: An ultrasound is for unexplained or progressive CKD, haematuria or suspected obstruction, not for confirming early albuminuria with a normal eGFR.
A timed 24-hour collection is awkward and less reliable than repeat spot uACR, and no longer advised for screening or confirmation.
Electrophoresis looks for a paraprotein (myeloma), which is not suggested by isolated albuminuria in long-standing diabetes.
A biopsy is kept for atypical features such as rapid eGFR decline, active sediment or no retinopathy, not for unconfirmed moderate albuminuria.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman, not breastfeeding, has a red retroareolar lump unresolved after five days of flucloxacillin. Ultrasound shows an abscess and a separate irregular, vascular solid mass with angular margins.
questions.ask: Most appropriate next step for the mass?
questions.explanation: The collection is the abscess, but the separate irregular, vascular solid mass with angular margins looks malignant and an abscess cannot explain it. In a non-lactational infection that has not responded to antibiotics, this mass needs a tissue diagnosis, and core biopsy is the preferred method to complete triple assessment.
why: FNA cytology cannot reliably tell invasive from in situ cancer and gives no receptor status, so core biopsy is preferred.
Waiting for the infection to settle gives false reassurance and delays the diagnosis of a mass that already looks malignant.
Incision and drainage would treat only the collection, and for a small abscess ultrasound-guided aspiration is preferred anyway.
MRI does not give a tissue diagnosis, and tissue is what this suspicious mass needs next.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old girl is on the paediatric ward of a regional hospital, 6 hours after treatment began for severe diabetic ketoacidosis at the first presentation of type 1 diabetes. At presentation she weighed 40 kg. Her venous pH was 7.02, bicarbonate 3 mmol/L, glucose 41.0 mmol/L, sodium 130 mmol/L and urea 14.2 mmol/L. She received a 10 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus, then fluids to replace her deficit over 48 hours with added potassium. An insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour was started after the first hour. She now has a severe headache, has vomited once, and is irritable and disorientated. Her temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 64/min (previously 128/min), blood pressure 134/86 mm Hg (previously 106/64 mm Hg), respirations 20/min and SpO2 98% on room air. Her GCS is 13 (E3 V4 M6). Her pupils are equal and reactive. Capillary glucose is 15.8 mmol/L and serum sodium is 134 mmol/L.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Non-contrast CT brain before any further treatment
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg over 1 hour
Increase the fluid rate to replace the deficit over 24 hours
Intravenous mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg over 20 minutes
questions.explanation: This girl has cerebral oedema, the main cause of death in children with DKA. She has several risk factors: a first presentation, young age, severe acidosis and a high urea at presentation. It typically appears 4 to 12 hours into treatment. The warning signs are a new headache, vomiting, irritability or confusion, a falling GCS, and a falling heart rate with rising blood pressure (part of the Cushing response). The RCH DKA guideline and ISPAD 2022 say to treat on clinical grounds straight away. Give IV mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg over 20 minutes, or 3% hypertonic saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg over 10 to 15 minutes. At the same time, cut the fluid rate by one third, raise the head of the bed, call senior and intensive care help, and arrange retrieval or transfer. Imaging comes only after she is stable. CT brain should not delay treatment, because a normal early scan does not rule out cerebral oedema and she could herniate while waiting for it. Bicarbonate is itself linked to cerebral oedema and has no role here. Faster fluids would make the brain swelling worse. Her glucose of 15.8 mmol/L rules out hypoglycaemia as the cause of her confusion.
why: Wrong: imaging must not delay treatment, because cerebral oedema is diagnosed clinically and an early CT may be normal; scan only once she is stable.
Wrong: bicarbonate in paediatric DKA is linked to cerebral oedema and is not indicated; her acidosis is improving with insulin and fluids.
Wrong: giving fluid faster makes cerebral oedema worse; the fluid rate should be cut by one third, not increased.
Wrong: her capillary glucose is 15.8 mmol/L, so hypoglycaemia does not explain her confusion, and the change in her heart rate and blood pressure points to raised intracranial pressure.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 35 weeks 4 days' gestation comes to the maternity assessment unit because her baby has moved much less than usual since the previous evening. Two years ago she had a stillbirth at 38 weeks, and that infant was small for gestational age. In this pregnancy she has diet-controlled gestational diabetes. A scan at 32 weeks showed an estimated weight on the 40th centile. She takes low-dose aspirin. Her blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg, pulse is 86/min, respirations are 16/min and temperature is 36.7 °C. Symphysis-fundal height is 35 cm. A urine dipstick shows no protein. A 40-minute cardiotocograph (CTG) shows a baseline rate of 135 bpm, baseline variability of 10 bpm, three accelerations of at least 15 bpm lasting at least 15 seconds, and no decelerations. She feels several movements during the trace.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Same-day sonographic biometry and liquor volume assessment
Discharge with routine antenatal review at 37 weeks
Continuation of the CTG for a further 40 minutes
questions.explanation: Every feature of this CTG is normal by RANZCOG criteria: the baseline is 110 to 160 bpm, variability is 6 to 25 bpm, there are accelerations and there are no decelerations. Her observations and urinalysis show no sign of pre-eclampsia or infection. A normal CTG means the fetus is not hypoxic right now. It does not rule out underlying placental insufficiency or growth restriction, so it does not exclude a later poor outcome. The Stillbirth CRE guideline on decreased fetal movements says that when a woman has risk factors for growth restriction or stillbirth, she should have an ultrasound for fetal biometry and amniotic fluid volume, ideally within 24 hours, along with obstetric review. This woman has a previous small-for-gestational-age stillbirth and gestational diabetes. The scan should be arranged today. She should then be told to come back straight away, at any hour, if movements decrease again.
why: Sending her home with routine follow-up treats the normal CTG as if it rules out compromise, which is unsafe in a woman with risk factors for stillbirth.
A single episode of reduced movements with a normal CTG and a normal assessment is not a reason for birth at 35 weeks, and preterm induction brings neonatal risks with no proven benefit.
The trace already meets every normal criterion with a good signal, so recording for longer adds no information about her placental reserve.
A Kleihauer-Betke test looks for fetomaternal haemorrhage, which would be suspected with a sinusoidal or abnormal trace, trauma or bleeding, and none of these is present here.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman is brought in after a high-speed car crash, breathless with BP 82/50 mmHg. Her trachea deviates left and the right chest is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds.
questions.ask: Most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: She has a right tension pneumothorax with obstructive shock. This is diagnosed on clinical signs and needs immediate decompression, by needle at the 4th or 5th intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line or by finger thoracostomy. An intercostal catheter on an underwater seal follows.
why: Tension pneumothorax is diagnosed clinically, and waiting for a film in a hypotensive patient wastes critical time.
Tamponade does not cause tracheal deviation or a hyper-resonant hemithorax with absent breath sounds on one side.
Positive-pressure ventilation before decompression makes the tension worse and can cause cardiac arrest.
A hyper-resonant chest points to trapped air rather than haemothorax, and fluid will not relieve obstructive shock.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has left-sided ulcerative colitis confirmed on colonoscopy. Symptoms began 3 months ago. Liver function tests are normal. She asks about bowel cancer risk.
questions.ask: When should surveillance colonoscopy begin?
questions.explanation: Colorectal cancer risk in ulcerative colitis goes up with how long the disease has lasted and how much of the colon is involved. Australian guidelines (Cancer Council Australia, GESA) advise a first surveillance colonoscopy about 8 years after symptoms began. The interval after that depends on her risk, for example whether she has PSC, active inflammation, strictures or a family history.
why: Yearly colonoscopy from diagnosis is for patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis, and her normal liver tests make PSC unlikely.
Waiting 15 years would miss the period when dysplasia and cancer risk are already rising.
Age 45 is the starting age for average-risk population screening, and it does not apply to colitis-related risk.
Age 50 is an older population screening age that ignores how long she has had colitis, so cancer could be found late.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man has two days of sharp chest pain eased by sitting forward, following a cold. ECG shows diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression; troponin is normal. Ibuprofen is started.
questions.ask: Which added drug most reduces recurrence?
questions.explanation: Recurrence is the commonest complication of acute pericarditis and happens in up to about 30% of patients. Under eTG and the 2025 ESC guidelines, colchicine for 3 months is added to an NSAID: 500 micrograms once daily under 70 kg, or twice daily from 70 kg. It roughly halves the recurrence rate and speeds symptom relief.
why: Corticosteroids are not first-line, and early use in viral or idiopathic pericarditis actually raises the risk of recurrence.
Hydroxychloroquine is used for lupus serositis, which has not been shown here, and it does not prevent recurrence of viral or idiopathic pericarditis.
Beta-blockers may ease the tachycardia, but they do nothing to the pericardial inflammation or the recurrence risk.
A proton pump inhibitor is given as gastroprotection with the NSAID, but it does not change the risk of recurrence.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman has central chest tightness, now settled with GTN. BP 136/80 mmHg. ECG shows new lateral ST depression; hs-troponin T rises from 40 to 115 ng/L.
questions.ask: Most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: She has a high-risk NSTEMI: no ST elevation, but dynamic ST depression and a rising troponin above the 99th percentile. Australian ACS guidelines recommend invasive coronary angiography within 24 hours, alongside aspirin, a P2Y12 inhibitor and an anticoagulant. Her pain has settled and she is haemodynamically stable, so the very-high-risk 2-hour pathway does not apply.
why: The 2-hour pathway is for very-high-risk features such as refractory pain, haemodynamic instability, acute heart failure or a life-threatening arrhythmia, and she has none of these.
Thrombolysis is used only for STEMI when PCI cannot be done in time, and it does not help in NSTEMI.
Stress testing is for low-risk chest pain with negative troponins and a normal ECG, not for a confirmed NSTEMI.
CT coronary angiography is used to rule out disease in low- to intermediate-risk patients, not to plan revascularisation in a confirmed NSTEMI.

questions.stem:
A 57-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after vomiting about 400 mL of bright red blood at home. He has passed black stools for 2 days. He has drunk about 10 standard drinks of beer daily for 20 years, and his last drink was last night. He takes no regular medicines. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse is 116/min, respirations are 20/min, blood pressure is 100/62 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. He is alert and oriented. He has spider naevi on his chest and palmar erythema. The abdomen has shifting dullness, and the spleen tip is palpable. Two large-bore cannulas are inserted and a crystalloid bolus is started. Laboratory studies show:
Haemoglobin 88 g/L (130–180)
Platelets 74 x10^9/L (150–400)
INR 1.9 (0.9–1.2)
Urea 12.4 mmol/L (2.5–7.5)
Creatinine 90 µmol/L (60–110)
Albumin 26 g/L (35–50)
The gastroenterology registrar plans endoscopy within the next few hours.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Fresh frozen plasma to correct the INR
Pantoprazole infusion as the only drug therapy
Red cell transfusion to a haemoglobin above 100 g/L
questions.explanation: This man has an upper GI bleed with features of decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis and portal hypertension: ascites, splenomegaly, stigmata of chronic liver disease, low platelets, a raised INR and a low albumin. His tachycardia and borderline blood pressure point to significant blood loss. The bleed should be treated as variceal until endoscopy shows otherwise. Under Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG) and Baveno VII, a vasoactive drug (terlipressin 2 mg IV every 4 hours, or octreotide) should start as soon as a variceal bleed is suspected, before endoscopy. It lowers portal pressure, improves control of bleeding and reduces mortality. Patients with cirrhosis and GI bleeding should also get antibiotic prophylaxis (ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily). This reduces bacterial infection, rebleeding and death. Endoscopic band ligation should follow within 12 hours. Fresh frozen plasma is wrong because the INR does not reflect bleeding risk in cirrhosis, and the extra volume can raise portal pressure. A pantoprazole infusion alone is wrong because it does nothing for a variceal bleed and would delay vasoactive therapy and antibiotics. Transfusing to a haemoglobin above 100 g/L is wrong because the restrictive target is 70 to 80 g/L, and over-transfusion raises portal pressure and the risk of rebleeding. Balloon tamponade is wrong at this stage because it is a temporary bridge for bleeding that cannot be controlled after drug and endoscopic therapy.
why: Fresh frozen plasma is wrong because the INR does not predict bleeding in cirrhosis, eTG advises against routinely correcting it, and the extra volume raises portal pressure.
A pantoprazole infusion alone is wrong because it does not lower portal pressure or treat a variceal bleed, and it leaves out the vasoactive drug and antibiotics the guidelines require.
Transfusing to a haemoglobin above 100 g/L is wrong because the restrictive target is 70 to 80 g/L, and over-transfusion raises portal pressure and the risk of rebleeding.
Balloon tamponade is wrong because it is only a temporary rescue for bleeding that cannot be controlled after drug and endoscopic therapy, and endoscopy is already planned.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes and newly diagnosed Hashimoto thyroiditis reports fatigue. Haemoglobin is 101 g/L and MCV 120 fL. B12 and folate results are pending.
questions.ask: Greatest risk of starting folic acid alone?
questions.explanation: An MCV of 120 fL is too high to blame on hypothyroidism alone. Her two autoimmune diseases make pernicious anaemia likely. Folic acid alone can correct the anaemia while the B12 deficiency goes on damaging nerves, so subacute combined degeneration of the cord can appear or get worse. B12 deficiency must be excluded or treated before folate is given.
why: Hypokalaemia comes from the rapid red cell production after B12 replacement in severe anaemia, not from folate given to a patient with a mild anaemia.
A rise in platelets during recovery from megaloblastic anaemia is a harmless lab finding, not the main danger.
Folic acid has no effect on glucose levels or insulin needs, so it does not cause hypoglycaemia.
Folic acid has no effect on the thyroid; thyrotoxicosis would come from too much levothyroxine, not from folate.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man with newly diagnosed ileocolonic Crohn's disease has haemoglobin 118 g/L, MCV 76 fL, ferritin 16 µg/L, transferrin saturation 8% and CRP 28 mg/L.
questions.ask: Most likely cause of his anaemia?
questions.explanation: Ferritin is an acute phase reactant, so inflammation pushes it up. A ferritin of 16 µg/L with a CRP of 28 mg/L therefore confirms true iron deficiency, and the microcytosis and low transferrin saturation support this. In active IBD, IV iron is preferred.
why: Anaemia of inflammation is usually normocytic with a normal or high ferritin (often above 100 µg/L), not a ferritin of 16 µg/L.
Thalassaemia trait causes microcytosis with normal iron stores, so it would not explain the low ferritin and transferrin saturation.
Ileal Crohn's disease can cause B12 deficiency, but that gives a macrocytic anaemia, and here the MCV is 76 fL.
Sideroblastic anaemia shows iron overload, with high ferritin and transferrin saturation, which is the opposite of these results.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man presents to a general practice in Perth with a 7-week history of cough productive of yellow phlegm. For the past week the phlegm has been streaked with blood. He reports drenching night sweats and has lost 6 kg without trying. He was born in the Philippines, moved to Australia 4 years ago and works as a cleaner. He has no medical history, takes no regular medicines and has never smoked. His temperature is 37.9 °C, heart rate 96/min, respiratory rate 18/min, blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. There are crackles over the left upper zone, and there is no clubbing or lymphadenopathy. White cell count is 8.4 x10^9/L (4.0–11.0), CRP is 41 mg/L (<5) and HIV serology is negative. A chest X-ray shows patchy opacification with a small cavity at the left apex. He has been given a surgical mask and moved to a separate room.
questions.ask: Which of the following investigations is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Interferon-gamma release assay on peripheral blood
Tuberculin skin test read at 48 to 72 hours
Three sputum samples for acid-fast smear, culture and NAAT
Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest
questions.explanation: This man has had a productive cough for more than 3 weeks, with haemoptysis, night sweats and weight loss. He was born in a country with high TB rates, and his chest X-ray shows a cavity in the upper lobe. This is active pulmonary tuberculosis until proven otherwise. The X-ray supports the diagnosis but cannot confirm it. Confirmation needs microbiology. The Australian guidelines (CDNA SoNG, the state TB programs and eTG Antibiotic) recommend 3 sputum samples collected at least 8 hours apart, with at least 1 taken first thing in the morning. Each sample has acid-fast bacilli smear microscopy, mycobacterial culture and a nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT, such as Xpert MTB/RIF). Smear microscopy and NAAT give a quick answer. NAAT also tells M. tuberculosis apart from non-tuberculous mycobacteria and detects rifampicin resistance. Culture is the gold standard and gives full drug-susceptibility results. A cavity usually means a high bacterial load, so expectorated sputum is very likely to be positive. The samples should be collected outdoors or in a well-ventilated room, away from other people. He also needs urgent referral to the state TB service and notification.
why: An interferon-gamma release assay shows immune sensitisation to M. tuberculosis, but it cannot tell latent infection from active disease, and a negative result does not exclude active TB.
A tuberculin skin test cannot tell latent infection from active disease, can be falsely positive after BCG vaccination (common in people born in the Philippines), and needs a second visit.
CT shows the cavity and the extent of disease in more detail, but it provides no microbiological confirmation or susceptibility results and does not change the need for sputum testing.

Bronchoscopy with lavage is invasive and carries a risk of spreading infection to staff, so it is kept for patients who cannot produce sputum or whose sputum samples are negative despite strong suspicion.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman with one previous vaginal birth is being induced at 40 weeks. Cervix 3 cm dilated, vertex 4/5 palpable at station -3. Amniotomy is planned.
questions.ask: Which complication is she at greatest risk of?
questions.explanation: If the membranes are ruptured while the presenting part is high and not engaged, the cord can slip past the head and be compressed. Queensland induction guidance and the RCOG cord prolapse guideline advise against amniotomy with a high head where possible. If it must be done, the fetal heart should be checked straight afterwards, and any sudden deceleration needs a vaginal examination to look for the cord.
why: Abruption after amniotomy mainly happens when a lot of fluid drains suddenly in polyhydramnios, and she has no polyhydramnios.
Uterine rupture is mainly a risk with a uterine scar or obstructed labour, and she has only had a vaginal birth.
Amniotic fluid embolism is very rare and unpredictable, so amniotomy does not make it the main risk for her.
Tachysystole is caused by too much oxytocin or prostaglandin, not by amniotomy itself.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 2 days of left-sided temporal headache. She has pain when brushing her hair and jaw pain that builds while chewing and settles at rest. This morning she woke with a grey shadow over the lower half of the vision in her left eye. She has hypertension treated with perindopril and has never had regular headaches. Her temperature is 37.3°C, pulse is 82/min, respirations are 16/min, blood pressure is 148/86 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. The left temporal artery is thickened, tender and pulseless. Visual acuity is 6/6 in the right eye and 6/24 in the left. There is a left relative afferent pupillary defect, and fundoscopy shows a pale, swollen left optic disc. ESR is 92 mm/h (reference <30), CRP is 64 mg/L (reference <5) and platelet count is 498 × 10^9/L (reference 150–400).
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Non-contrast CT scan of the brain
Oral aspirin 300 mg as a single dose
questions.explanation: This woman over 50 has a new temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, a thickened pulseless temporal artery, raised ESR and CRP, and thrombocytosis. This is giant cell arteritis. Her left eye shows reduced acuity, an inferior field defect, an RAPD and a pale (chalky) swollen disc, so she already has arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy. Without treatment, the other eye can lose vision within days. Therapeutic Guidelines (Rheumatology) advise that suspected GCA with any visual symptom or sign is a sight-threatening emergency. It should be treated at once with IV methylprednisolone 500 mg to 1 g daily for 3 days, then high-dose oral prednisolone, with same-day ophthalmology review. Treatment should never wait for a biopsy or imaging. Oral prednisolone 50 mg daily is the starting dose for GCA without visual involvement and is not enough once the optic nerve is ischaemic. A temporal artery biopsy confirms the diagnosis, but it stays positive for 1 to 2 weeks after steroids start, so waiting for it only risks the other eye. A CT brain is not needed: the headache came on gradually, there are no focal deficits, the picture is classic GCA, and the scan would delay treatment. Aspirin does not treat the vasculitis and cannot replace corticosteroids.
why: Oral prednisolone 40 to 60 mg is the right start for GCA without visual involvement, but she already has ischaemic optic neuropathy and needs IV pulse therapy.
A biopsy stays diagnostic for 1 to 2 weeks after steroids start, so it should be done after treatment begins, not before.
A gradual-onset headache with no focal neurological signs and classic GCA features does not need CT, and scanning first would delay sight-saving treatment.
Aspirin does not suppress the granulomatous vasculitis and cannot replace urgent high-dose corticosteroids.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman has 3 months of loose stools, bloating and fatigue. Ferritin is 5 µg/L. tTG-IgA is 180 U/mL (normal <20) with normal total IgA; she still eats gluten.
questions.ask: Most appropriate next investigation?

In Australian adults, GESA and Coeliac Australia still require confirmation by gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies (at least 4 from D2 and 1 to 2 from the bulb) while the patient is eating gluten, before a lifelong gluten-free diet is started.
why: Colonoscopy does not sample the proximal small bowel, where coeliac disease causes its damage.
HLA-DQ2/DQ8 typing is mainly useful to rule coeliac disease out, because many healthy people carry these alleles, so a positive result cannot confirm it.
Faecal calprotectin helps tell inflammatory bowel disease from IBS, and it does not confirm coeliac disease.
Capsule endoscopy is kept for complicated or refractory coeliac disease, or for patients who cannot have a gastroscopy, and it does not give tissue for histology.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman is reviewed in the coronary care unit 3 hours after emergency coronary angiography. She came to the emergency department with central chest pain, fever and a productive cough 2 days after her sister's funeral. Her ECG showed ST elevation in V2 to V4. Angiography showed no obstructive coronary disease, and left ventriculography showed apical ballooning. Her chest X-ray shows right lower lobe pneumonia, and she is receiving ceftriaxone and azithromycin. She has had 1 L of crystalloid since arrival. Temperature is 38.2 °C, pulse 108/min, blood pressure 82/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min and SpO2 95% on 2 L/min oxygen. She has a new harsh systolic murmur at the left sternal edge. Her JVP is not raised, and there are crackles at the right base only. Bedside echocardiography shows an LVEF of 35%, apical akinesis with hyperdynamic basal segments, systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve and a peak left ventricular outflow tract gradient of 70 mmHg. Serum lactate is 2.9 mmol/L (reference below 2.0).
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in managing her low blood pressure?
questions.explanation: This woman has Takotsubo cardiomyopathy: two stress triggers (her sister's death and pneumonia with sepsis), apical ballooning, and no culprit lesion on angiography. She now has one of its most dangerous complications, dynamic left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction. The basal segments contract too hard, which pulls the anterior mitral leaflet into the outflow tract (systolic anterior motion, SAM). That causes the new systolic murmur, a gradient of 70 mmHg and hypotension. The obstruction gets worse with anything that empties the ventricle or makes it contract harder: low preload, low afterload, tachycardia or inotropes. Her JVP is not raised, she has no pulmonary oedema, and sepsis has left her relatively low on fluid, so the first step is a cautious crystalloid bolus to fill the LV and widen the outflow tract. Reassess after each bolus. If hypotension persists, the next options are a pure vasoconstrictor such as phenylephrine, a short-acting beta-blocker if she can tolerate it, or mechanical support that does not lower afterload. Inotropes are avoided. This is the key safety point after Takotsubo is diagnosed in a shocked patient: get an echo to look for an LVOT gradient before giving any inotrope.
why: Wrong: dobutamine is an inotrope that makes the basal segments contract harder and speeds the heart, which worsens SAM, raises the LVOT gradient and can deepen the shock.
Wrong: a nitrate dilates veins and arteries, lowering preload and afterload, which narrows the outflow tract, worsens the obstruction and would drop her blood pressure further.
Wrong: a diuretic lowers preload in a woman with no pulmonary oedema and a JVP that is not raised, so the LV cavity shrinks and the obstruction gets worse.
Wrong: a balloon pump lowers afterload, which can increase the LVOT gradient, so it is not recommended in Takotsubo with outflow obstruction.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of burning central chest pain that began 90 minutes after a large dinner. For 6 weeks he has had similar pain on most evenings. It is worse when he lies flat and partly eased by over-the-counter antacids, and he has acid regurgitation. For the past month, bread and steak have felt as if they stick behind his sternum. His weight has fallen from 84 kg to 79 kg over 3 months without dieting. He drinks about 4 standard drinks daily, stopped smoking 10 years ago and takes no regular medicines. Temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse 82/min, blood pressure 134/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min and SpO2 98% on room air. He has mild epigastric tenderness and no palpable lymph nodes. A 12-lead ECG recorded during pain is normal. High-sensitivity troponin I is 2 ng/L at 0 hours and 2 ng/L at 2 hours (99th percentile 26 ng/L). Haemoglobin is 136 g/L (reference 130 to 180 g/L).
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

Urea breath test for Helicobacter pylori

A long-acting muscarinic antagonist such as tiotropium, taken once daily and kept alongside the as-needed reliever, is a standard first choice. It improves breathlessness, exercise tolerance and quality of life, and it reduces flare-ups. questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with 4 days of thirst, polyuria and weight loss, and 1 day of vomiting. He has no past medical history. He weighs 36 kg. His first venous blood gas shows pH 6.98, bicarbonate 4 mmol/L, glucose 34.0 mmol/L and sodium 131 mmol/L. Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate is 6.8 mmol/L and urea is 13.2 mmol/L. Fluid replacement is started, and 1 hour later an insulin infusion is started at 0.1 units/kg/h. Five hours after arrival he says he has a severe headache, vomits, and becomes irritable and confused. His pulse is 58/min (130/min on arrival), blood pressure is 142/90 mm Hg, respirations are 26/min, SpO2 is 98% on room air and temperature is 36.9 °C. GCS is 11 (E3 V3 M5). His pupils are equal and reactive. Repeat glucose is 15.2 mmol/L and sodium is 129 mmol/L. The head of the bed is raised and the fluid rate is reduced.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Non-contrast CT scan of the brain now
Sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg IV over 1 hour
Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg IV as a single dose
Cease the insulin infusion until review
questions.explanation: This boy has severe DKA as his first presentation of type 1 diabetes. He has the main risk factors for cerebral oedema: young age, new diagnosis, pH below 7.1, a high urea, and a sodium that is falling instead of rising as the glucose comes down. Several hours into treatment he has a headache, vomiting, a falling GCS and a new low heart rate with high blood pressure (Cushing response). This is a clinical diagnosis of cerebral oedema. The RCH DKA guideline says to treat it straight away, without waiting for imaging. Raise the head of the bed, reduce the fluid rate, and give mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg (2.5 to 5 mL/kg of 20%) IV over 20 minutes. Hypertonic 3% saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg is an alternative. Call ICU early for airway support, and do a CT only after he is stable, to look for other causes such as a clot or bleed. CT now is wrong because imaging delays treatment that can save his life, and cerebral oedema is diagnosed clinically. Sodium bicarbonate is wrong because it does not improve outcomes in DKA and is itself linked to cerebral oedema. Dexamethasone is wrong because steroids do not help this kind of brain swelling and they make hyperglycaemia worse. Stopping the insulin is wrong because the ketosis needs ongoing insulin to clear; the rate may be lowered, but the infusion should not be stopped to treat cerebral oedema.
why: Wrong: CT delays urgent treatment for a diagnosis made clinically; image only once he is stable.
Wrong: bicarbonate does not improve outcomes in DKA and is itself a risk factor for cerebral oedema.
Wrong: corticosteroids have no role in cerebral oedema from DKA and would worsen his hyperglycaemia.
Wrong: insulin is still needed to clear the ketosis, and stopping it does not treat the raised intracranial pressure.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after a sudden, severe occipital headache that began while he was jogging. Two weeks ago he had a severe headache that settled within 30 minutes. He has autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease and hypertension, treated with perindopril. On arrival, his temperature is 37.3 °C, pulse 82/min, respirations 16/min, blood pressure 140/85 mm Hg and SpO2 98% on room air. His Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is 13 (E3 V4 M6). He has neck stiffness and bilateral subhyaloid haemorrhages on fundoscopy, and no focal deficit. INR is 1.0 and platelets are 245 x10^9/L. Non-contrast CT shows diffuse blood in the basal cisterns, spreading into the ventricles, with dilated temporal horns. CT angiography shows a 7 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm. Forty-five minutes later he vomits. His GCS is now 11 (E3 V3 M5), pulse 48/min, blood pressure 204/96 mm Hg and respirations 12/min and irregular. His pupils are still equal and reactive.
questions.ask: Which of the following best explains the change in his vital signs?
questions.explanation: This man has an aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage. Blood has spread into his ventricles, and the dilated temporal horns show early hydrocephalus. Since arrival his GCS has fallen. He now has a rising systolic pressure, a slow heart rate and irregular breathing. This is Cushing's triad, a late sign that intracranial pressure is raised and the brainstem is being compressed, which means coning is imminent. Equal pupils do not rule this out, because pupil changes can come late. Do not read the rising blood pressure as something to treat on its own. It is the brain's attempt to keep up cerebral perfusion pressure, and lowering it hard could make ischaemia worse. Under eTG guidance and the Between the Flags criteria, this needs an immediate rapid response call, airway assessment, the head of the bed raised to 30 degrees, and an urgent neurosurgical review for an external ventricular drain. Delayed cerebral ischaemia usually happens on days 3 to 14, not within hours of the bleed. A hypertensive emergency does not explain the slow heart rate or the fall in GCS, and on arrival his blood pressure was only 140/85 mm Hg. A vagal response to vomiting slows the heart but lowers the blood pressure. Neurogenic stunned myocardium from a catecholamine surge typically causes a fast heart rate, low blood pressure and heart failure.
why: Wrong: delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm typically happens on days 3 to 14 after the bleed, not 3 hours after the headache began.
Wrong: a hypertensive emergency would not cause a falling heart rate or irregular breathing, and his blood pressure was only 140/85 mm Hg before his GCS fell.
Wrong: a vagal response to vomiting slows the heart but lowers the blood pressure, and it would not cause a lasting fall in GCS or irregular breathing.
Wrong: neurogenic stunned myocardium from a catecholamine surge usually causes a fast heart rate, low blood pressure and pulmonary oedema, not a slow heart rate with severe hypertension.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man is on the cardiology ward of a regional hospital, waiting for transfer for coronary angiography. He was admitted 18 hours ago with a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction and has no pain now. Overnight telemetry has shown frequent multifocal ventricular ectopic beats and two runs of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, each 5 to 7 beats long. He has hypertension treated with indapamide. Since admission he has been given aspirin, ticagrelor, therapeutic enoxaparin, metoprolol and atorvastatin. His blood pressure is 128/76 mmHg, pulse 78/min and regular, respiratory rate 16/min and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Heart sounds are normal and the chest is clear. A 12-lead ECG shows sinus rhythm, 1 mm ST depression in V4 to V6 and a QTc of 470 ms. Results: hs-troponin I 1960 ng/L (less than 26), K+ 3.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), Mg2+ 0.58 mmol/L (0.70 to 1.10), creatinine 90 µmol/L (60 to 110).
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate measure to reduce his risk of ventricular fibrillation before angiography?
options: Intravenous amiodarone loading dose, then maintenance infusion
Intravenous magnesium sulfate, then potassium chloride infusion
Intravenous lidocaine bolus, then prophylactic infusion
Oral slow-release potassium chloride tablets alone
Oral flecainide twice daily until angiography
questions.explanation: This man has an evolving NSTEMI and is waiting for angiography. Ventricular ectopy and non-sustained VT on telemetry, a borderline long QTc, and low potassium and magnesium from his thiazide-like diuretic (indapamide) put him at high risk of ventricular fibrillation. In acute coronary syndrome, Australian ACS guidance and ANZCOR advise correcting electrolytes promptly, aiming for potassium of at least 4.0 mmol/L (4.0 to 5.0) and magnesium of at least 1.0 mmol/L. Give magnesium first, for example magnesium sulfate 10 to 20 mmol IV over about an hour. Low magnesium makes low potassium hard to correct, because the kidneys keep losing potassium, and magnesium also stabilises the myocardium when the QT is long. Then give IV potassium chloride at a safe ward rate (for example 10 mmol/h through a peripheral line) with ECG monitoring, recheck the levels, and stop the indapamide. Keep him on continuous monitoring, continue the beta-blocker, and arrange early angiography to treat the ischaemic cause. Prophylactic antiarrhythmic drugs are not recommended in ACS.
why: Prophylactic amiodarone for asymptomatic non-sustained VT after myocardial infarction does not lower mortality and is not recommended; amiodarone is kept for sustained or recurrent haemodynamically important VT, or for refractory VF during cardiac arrest.
Prophylactic lidocaine in acute myocardial infarction reduces VF but increases mortality, mainly from asystole, so it is no longer used.
Oral potassium alone works too slowly in a patient at high arrhythmic risk, and it does not correct the low magnesium that will keep the potassium from rising.
Flecainide, a class Ic drug, is contraindicated in ischaemic heart disease because it increased arrhythmic death after myocardial infarction in the CAST trial.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man, an electrician, sees his general practitioner because of 5 months of daytime sleepiness. He dozes off while watching television and in the afternoons, and he wakes unrefreshed despite 8 hours in bed. His wife reports loud snoring every night, with pauses in his breathing followed by gasping. He has had no sudden muscle weakness with laughter or anger, and he denies sleepiness while driving. He drinks 3 standard drinks most evenings and does not smoke. He has hypertension treated with perindopril. Blood pressure is 146/92 mm Hg, heart rate 76/min and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. BMI is 34 kg/m2, neck circumference is 44 cm and the oropharynx is crowded. His Epworth Sleepiness Scale score is 13 (normal 10 or less), STOP-Bang score 6/8 and OSA50 score 7/10. Full blood count, TSH and electrolytes are normal.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: This man very probably has obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA). He snores, his wife has seen him stop breathing, he is sleepy in the daytime, he has obesity with a large neck and a crowded oropharynx, he has hypertension, and he drinks alcohol in the evening. Before treatment starts, the diagnosis has to be confirmed and graded by the apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI). His Epworth score is 8 or more and his STOP-Bang (4 or more) and OSA50 (5 or more) scores are high-risk. This meets the MBS item 12250 criteria, so a GP can refer him directly for an unattended Level 2 polysomnography done at home. Australasian Sleep Association and eTG guidance say this test is the right one for a patient with a high pre-test probability and no major other illness. Treatment then depends on the AHI: CPAP is first line for moderate to severe OSA, and everyone gets lifestyle measures (weight loss, less alcohol, side sleeping) and advice on driving. Overnight oximetry alone misses hypopnoeas that do not lower oxygen levels and cannot measure the AHI, so it is not enough to diagnose OSA. CPAP, a splint or a wake-promoting drug should not be started before the diagnosis and severity are known.
why: Oximetry alone cannot measure the AHI and misses hypopnoeas that do not lower oxygen levels, so it is not recommended for diagnosing OSA.
CPAP is first line only once a sleep study has confirmed moderate to severe OSA, and it should not be started on screening scores alone.
A mandibular advancement splint is an alternative for confirmed mild to moderate OSA or for people who cannot tolerate CPAP, so it is not a first step before diagnosis.
Modafinil is used only for sleepiness that persists despite adequate treatment of confirmed OSA, and it does nothing for the airway obstruction.

questions.stem: A 6-week-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his father with 4 days of forceful vomiting after every feed. The vomit is milky and has never been green. He feeds eagerly straight after vomiting and has had 2 wet nappies in the past 24 hours. He was born at term and is formula fed. He weighs 4.5 kg, down from 4.9 kg 2 weeks ago. Temperature is 36.8°C, pulse 172/min, respirations 38/min, blood pressure 84/50 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He is drowsy but rouses to voice. His hands and feet are cool and capillary refill time is 3 seconds. A peripheral cannula is placed. Venous gas: pH 7.53 (7.32 to 7.42), bicarbonate 37 mmol/L (20 to 28), lactate 1.1 mmol/L (under 2.0), Na 133 mmol/L (135 to 145), K 2.9 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), Cl 86 mmol/L (95 to 110), glucose 4.3 mmol/L. Ultrasound shows a pyloric muscle thickness of 5 mm and a channel length of 18 mm.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: 0.45% sodium chloride with 2.5% glucose at 18 mL/h intravenously
0.9% sodium chloride 45 mL intravenously over 15 minutes
Potassium chloride 2.25 mmol intravenously over 1 hour
Hydrocortisone 25 mg intravenously as a single dose
Laparoscopic pyloromyotomy on the next available list
questions.explanation: This boy has hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. The ultrasound shows a muscle wall of 5 mm or more (abnormal is 3 mm or more) and a channel of 18 mm (abnormal is 15 mm or more), and he has the typical hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. He is also in compensated shock: he is tachycardic, drowsy and cool at the hands and feet, with a capillary refill time of 3 seconds, while his blood pressure is still normal. Pyloric stenosis is a medical emergency but a surgical urgency, not a surgical emergency. The first step is to treat the shock. Keep him nil by mouth and give a 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride (45 mL for 4.5 kg), then reassess. After that, give 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose for maintenance plus deficit, and add potassium once he is passing urine (RCH Pyloric stenosis, Dehydration and Intravenous fluids guidelines). Surgery waits until the bicarbonate and chloride are back to normal, because operating while he is still alkalotic risks apnoea after the anaesthetic.
why: Correct: compensated shock needs a 10 mL/kg isotonic bolus first, here 45 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride, with reassessment afterwards.
Wrong: potassium is replaced only after perfusion is restored and he is passing urine, and it does not treat the shock.
Wrong: his low potassium and alkalosis are the opposite of salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia, which causes a high potassium and an acidosis, so steroids are not needed.
Wrong: pyloromyotomy should wait until shock and the alkalosis are corrected, because operating sooner risks apnoea after the anaesthetic.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman, a school teacher, returns to her general practitioner for review of a duodenal ulcer. The rapid urease (CLO) result was positive, and antral biopsies showed Helicobacter pylori with no intestinal metaplasia or dysplasia. She ceased naproxen and yesterday completed 14 days of esomeprazole, amoxicillin and clarithromycin. She is now pain-free and is taking esomeprazole 20 mg daily to complete ulcer healing. She has no melaena or weight loss. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse 74/min and blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft and nontender. Haemoglobin is 136 g/L (reference 115–160 g/L).

Helicobacter pylori serology in 4 weeks, continuing the proton pump inhibitor
Faecal antigen test in 1 week, continuing the proton pump inhibitor
Repeat gastroscopy with biopsy in 8 weeks, off proton pump inhibitor
Urea breath test in 4 weeks, off proton pump inhibitor for the final 2 weeks

A faecal antigen test is a valid alternative only with the same timing rules, and at 1 week while she is still on the PPI it is unreliable. Testing 1 week after the antibiotics while she is still on a PPI is too early and risks a false-negative stool antigen result.
An uncomplicated duodenal ulcer with benign histology does not need repeat endoscopy; this invasive test is reserved for gastric or complicated ulcers.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department of a rural hospital by her daughter. She has had 4 days of worsening headache and, since this morning, new confusion. One week ago she tripped on a rug and hit the left side of her head on a door frame. She did not lose consciousness. She has atrial fibrillation and hypertension. Her medicines are rivaroxaban 20 mg daily, last taken at 07:00 today, and amlodipine. Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 76/min and irregular, blood pressure 166/88 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16/min and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Her GCS is 14 (E3 V5 M6) and falls to 13 (E3 V4 M6) over the next hour. Pupils are equal and reactive. She has a mild right pronator drift. INR is 1.2 (reference 0.9 to 1.3), APTT 32 seconds (reference 25 to 38), platelets 236 ×10^9/L and eGFR 72 mL/min/1.73 m². Non-contrast CT brain shows a crescentic, mixed-density left subdural collection 14 mm thick with 7 mm of midline shift. Neurosurgical retrieval has been requested.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management while she waits for transfer?
questions.explanation: This woman has an acute-on-subacute subdural haematoma while taking a factor Xa inhibitor. Her GCS is falling, she has a focal deficit and the CT shows mass effect. The biggest immediate risk is that the haematoma keeps growing and she herniates before she reaches neurosurgery. Reversing the anticoagulant is the most important step to prevent this. A normal INR and APTT do not rule out a clinically significant rivaroxaban effect, especially when the last dose was taken only hours ago and renal function is preserved. For life-threatening bleeding on apixaban or rivaroxaban, Therapeutic Guidelines recommend andexanet alfa where it is available and local protocol allows. Otherwise, give prothrombin complex concentrate (Prothrombinex-VF 50 units/kg IV) with haematology advice. Andexanet is rarely stocked in rural Australian hospitals, so Prothrombinex-VF is the appropriate choice here. Idarucizumab is wrong because it is a specific antibody fragment against dabigatran and has no effect on factor Xa inhibitors. Phytomenadione (vitamin K) is wrong because it reverses warfarin by restoring vitamin K-dependent factor synthesis, and it does nothing to a direct factor Xa inhibitor. Fresh frozen plasma is wrong because it provides too little clotting factor to overcome factor Xa inhibition, needs a large volume and takes time to thaw. Tranexamic acid is wrong because it is an antifibrinolytic that does not reverse rivaroxaban, and its trial benefit in traumatic brain injury applies only within 3 hours of injury, not a week later.
why: Idarucizumab binds only dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor, so it would not reverse rivaroxaban.

Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 92/min and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 168/94 mm Hg, respirations 16/min and SpO2 97% on room air. She has non-fluent aphasia, a right facial droop and right arm power of 1/5 (NIHSS 15). Capillary glucose is 7.2 mmol/L, platelets 241 x10^9/L (150-400), INR 1.1 (0.9-1.2) and APTT 30 seconds (25-38). Non-contrast CT brain shows no haemorrhage. CT angiography shows a left M1 occlusion, and CT perfusion shows a 10 mL core within a 90 mL perfusion deficit. An apixaban-specific anti-Xa level is pending.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: This woman has an acute left middle cerebral artery stroke from a proximal (M1) large vessel occlusion. She is within 6 hours of last known well, has a disabling deficit (NIHSS 15), and has a small core with a large salvageable penumbra. The Stroke Foundation Australian and New Zealand Living Clinical Guidelines recommend endovascular thrombectomy for anterior circulation large vessel occlusion in this setting, whether or not the patient can have thrombolysis. Anticoagulation does not rule it out. She took apixaban about 2 hours ago, well within 48 hours, so IV thrombolysis is contraindicated unless a drug-specific anti-Xa level shows no meaningful anticoagulant effect. A normal INR and APTT do not exclude a clinically relevant apixaban effect. Do not wait for the pending level before the clot retrieval pathway is started, because every minute of delay costs brain tissue. Other care in the meantime: keep her nil by mouth until a swallow screen, and do not lower blood pressure routinely. The value of 168/94 mm Hg is already below the 185/110 threshold used for reperfusion therapy.
why: Wrong: she took apixaban within 48 hours, and a normal INR and APTT do not exclude a significant apixaban effect, so thrombolysis carries an unacceptable risk of haemorrhage until a drug-specific level shows no effect.
Wrong: idarucizumab reverses only dabigatran and has no effect on apixaban, a factor Xa inhibitor.
Wrong: guidelines do not support reversing a DOAC with prothrombin complex concentrate so that thrombolysis can be given, as this adds thrombotic risk and delay without proven benefit.
Wrong: aspirin gives no reperfusion for a salvageable M1 occlusion, and adding an antiplatelet in a fully anticoagulated patient before reperfusion is decided raises bleeding risk.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 6 hours of worsening breathlessness, chest tightness and wheeze. She had an upper respiratory tract infection 4 days ago. She has had asthma since childhood. She uses only a reliever inhaler and has never been prescribed a preventer. On arrival she speaks in short phrases and is using her accessory muscles. Pulse is 118/min, respiratory rate 28/min, blood pressure 124/72 mm Hg, temperature 37.4 °C and SpO2 91% on room air. There is widespread expiratory wheeze. The trachea is central and air entry is equal on both sides. Over the first hour she receives oxygen by nasal prongs, salbutamol 12 puffs by spacer every 20 minutes, ipratropium 8 puffs by spacer every 20 minutes and oral prednisolone 50 mg. She is still alert but still speaks only in phrases. Pulse is 122/min, respiratory rate 27/min and SpO2 93% on 2 L/min oxygen. Wheeze persists. A chest X-ray shows hyperinflation with no pneumothorax or consolidation.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: This woman has acute severe asthma. She speaks only in phrases, uses her accessory muscles and has an SpO2 of 91% on room air. She has no features of life-threatening asthma: she is alert, with no cyanosis, no silent chest and no exhaustion. She has had an hour of optimal first-line treatment: repeated salbutamol by spacer, ipratropium, oral prednisolone and oxygen titrated to SpO2 92 to 96%. She is still in the severe category. The chest X-ray rules out a pneumothorax and consolidation. The Australian Asthma Handbook and eTG advise IV magnesium sulfate 10 mmol over 20 minutes for severe acute asthma that has not responded to first-line bronchodilators. She should keep having frequent salbutamol, and senior and ICU staff should be told. Aminophylline is not recommended as routine treatment because it adds little and causes arrhythmias and vomiting. IV hydrocortisone works no better than the oral prednisolone she has already had. IV salbutamol is kept for life-threatening asthma that does not respond, in a critical care setting. Nebulised adrenaline is for anaphylaxis or upper airway obstruction, not acute asthma. Before discharge she will need a preventer containing an inhaled corticosteroid and a written action plan.
why: Aminophylline is not recommended as routine treatment for acute asthma: it adds little bronchodilation to inhaled therapy and has a narrow therapeutic index, with arrhythmias, seizures and vomiting.
She has already had oral prednisolone 50 mg and can swallow, so IV hydrocortisone gives no extra benefit and repeats her corticosteroid.

An IV salbutamol infusion is kept for life-threatening asthma that does not respond to other treatment, in a critical care setting; it causes more tachycardia, lactic acidosis and hypokalaemia, and she has no life-threatening features.
Nebulised adrenaline treats anaphylaxis or upper airway obstruction such as croup, and she has no urticaria, angioedema, allergen exposure or stridor.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man comes to his general practitioner for review of heartburn. For 9 years he has had burning retrosternal pain after evening meals on most days, with sour fluid coming up into his throat when he lies down at night. He has treated it with over-the-counter antacids and has never seen a doctor about it. He has no difficulty swallowing, vomiting, black stools or weight loss. He has hypertension treated with perindopril. He smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 25 years and stopped 5 years ago. He drinks about 10 standard drinks of alcohol a week. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse is 72/min and blood pressure is 134/84 mm Hg. His BMI is 33 kg/m2 and his waist circumference is 110 cm. Abdominal examination is normal. A resting 12-lead ECG is normal. Haemoglobin is 146 g/L (reference 130–180 g/L) and ferritin is 120 µg/L (reference 30–500 µg/L).
questions.ask: Which of the following conditions is this patient at greatest risk of developing?
options: Squamous cell carcinoma of the oesophagus
questions.explanation: This man has had untreated gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) for 9 years, with typical burning retrosternal pain after meals and regurgitation at night. He also has most of the recognised risk factors for Barrett's oesophagus: male sex, age over 50, reflux for many years, nocturnal symptoms, central obesity and a history of smoking. In Barrett's oesophagus, repeated acid injury replaces the squamous lining of the distal oesophagus with columnar epithelium showing intestinal metaplasia. It causes no symptoms of its own, but it can progress through dysplasia to oesophageal adenocarcinoma, so it is the key complication to look for and counsel about. Cancer Council Australia and eTG guidance support gastroscopy for a man over 50 with chronic reflux and several Barrett's risk factors, even without alarm features. Management alongside this is lifestyle change (weight loss, smaller and earlier evening meals, raising the head of the bed) and a standard-dose PPI. If Barrett's is found, he needs endoscopic surveillance. Squamous cell carcinoma is linked to smoking and heavy alcohol use, not reflux. Eosinophilic oesophagitis and achalasia are not complications of GORD. Distal gastric adenocarcinoma is driven by Helicobacter pylori, not reflux.
why: Wrong: squamous cell carcinoma is mainly caused by heavy smoking and alcohol use, not acid reflux, and his moderate drinking and past smoking make it much less likely than reflux-driven metaplasia.
Wrong: eosinophilic oesophagitis is an allergic disorder that usually affects younger atopic men with dysphagia or food bolus impaction, and it is not a complication of long-standing reflux.
Wrong: achalasia is a primary motility disorder caused by loss of myenteric neurons, and it presents with progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids rather than developing from reflux.
Wrong: adenocarcinoma of the distal stomach is mainly linked to Helicobacter pylori and atrophic gastritis, not to acid reflux into the oesophagus.

GTN only relieves symptoms and does not reperfuse, and in inferior STEMI it can cause severe hypotension if the right ventricle is involved.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man is leaving the surgical ward on day 2 after laparoscopic appendicectomy with oxycodone 5 mg up to four times daily. He takes oral iron. Bowels not opened; abdomen soft.

A stool softener used alone does not counter the slowed gut movement caused by opioids, so it is not enough as prevention.
Peripheral opioid antagonists are kept for constipation that persists despite regular conventional laxatives, not for routine prevention.
A suppository is a rescue treatment for rectal loading, not a regular preventive regimen started with a new opioid.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman, para 2, is on the birth suite 25 minutes after a spontaneous vaginal birth at 38 weeks' gestation. Her labour was induced for pre-eclampsia. She received oxytocin 10 units at the birth, and the placenta and membranes were complete. She is now bleeding heavily with clots, and the measured loss is 1,300 mL. Bimanual compression has been done, a catheter has drained 450 mL of urine, an oxytocin infusion is running, and tranexamic acid 1 g IV was given 10 minutes ago. In labour she took oral labetalol and had a magnesium sulfate infusion. She has no history of asthma. Pulse is 122/min, blood pressure 104/66 mmHg (158/102 mmHg before the birth), respirations 24/min and SpO2 98% on oxygen 15 L/min by mask. The fundus is soft and above the umbilicus. Speculum examination shows no cervical or vaginal tear. Haemoglobin is 95 g/L, platelets 146 x 10^9/L and fibrinogen 3.4 g/L. Crossmatched blood has been requested.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: This is a major primary postpartum haemorrhage (1,300 mL with tachycardia) caused by uterine atony. The fundus is soft and high, and the other Ts have been checked: no tear (trauma), a complete placenta (tissue) and normal fibrinogen and near-normal platelets (thrombin). First-line measures are already done: uterine compression, an empty bladder, oxytocin IM then by infusion, and tranexamic acid. RANZCOG C-Obs 43 and Queensland Clinical Guidelines say the next step for ongoing atony is a second-line uterotonic. Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia because it can cause a hypertensive crisis, stroke or eclampsia, even though her BP has fallen from bleeding. Magnesium sulfate also adds to atony. She has no asthma, so carboprost (15-methyl PGF2-alpha) 250 micrograms IM is the right choice. It can be repeated every 15 minutes up to 8 doses (2 mg). Balloon tamponade and surgery are for bleeding that continues despite uterotonics.
why: Wrong: ergometrine is contraindicated in pre-eclampsia and hypertension because it can cause severe hypertension, stroke or eclampsia, and her current lower BP is from blood loss, not a resolved disease.
Wrong: misoprostol is slower in onset and less effective than other uterotonics, so guidelines keep it for when carboprost or ergometrine are unavailable or contraindicated.
Wrong: balloon tamponade is the next step only once uterotonics have failed, and she has not yet had a second-line uterotonic.
Wrong: laparotomy with a B-Lynch or similar suture is for haemorrhage that continues despite uterotonics and tamponade, so it is premature here.

questions.stem:
A 44-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 30 hours of constant right upper quadrant pain. It began after a fried dinner and radiates to her right shoulder. Over the past 8 months she has had brief, similar episodes after meals. Her temperature is 38.7 °C, pulse 106/min, blood pressure 126/80 mm Hg and SpO2 98% on room air. She is not jaundiced, and Murphy's sign is positive. Investigations show:
White cell count 13.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0)
CRP 88 mg/L (<5)
Total bilirubin 24 µmol/L (<20)
ALP 440 U/L (30-110)
GGT 210 U/L (<40)
ALT 31 U/L (<35)
Lipase 30 U/L (<60)
Ultrasound shows a gallbladder wall thickened to 5 mm, pericholecystic fluid and a stone impacted in the gallbladder neck. The common bile duct measures 5 mm, but bowel gas hides its distal end. She is given analgesia, IV fluids and IV antibiotics, and is admitted for laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation before surgery?
options: Repeat liver function tests in 6 weeks
questions.explanation: The ultrasound and inflammatory markers already show acute calculous cholecystitis. The question is what the liver function tests mean for her. A stone stuck in the cystic duct on its own usually causes only mild LFT changes. Her ALP and GGT are about 4 to 5 times the upper limit, with a normal ALT and a bilirubin that is only slightly raised. This cholestatic pattern suggests a common bile duct stone causing partial or intermittent blockage. A 5 mm duct and a bilirubin of 24 make complete obstruction unlikely, but they do not rule out a stone, especially since the distal duct could not be seen. That puts her at intermediate risk of choledocholithiasis. Guidelines (eTG, ASGE) recommend non-invasive duct imaging before cholecystectomy, either MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound, or else an intraoperative cholangiogram. ERCP is kept for a duct stone that has been confirmed, or for cholangitis that needs urgent drainage.
why: ERCP carries a risk of pancreatitis, bleeding and perforation, so it is used to treat a confirmed duct stone or cholangitis needing drainage rather than to look for a stone in a woman who is not jaundiced and has a non-dilated duct.
A HIDA scan tests whether the cystic duct is patent to diagnose cholecystitis, which the ultrasound has already confirmed, and it does not show stones in the common bile duct well.
CT misses many bile duct stones because cholesterol stones are often isodense with bile, and it adds radiation without answering the question the LFTs raise.
Waiting 6 weeks to repeat the LFTs would leave a possible duct stone unchecked through cholecystectomy during this admission, risking a retained stone, cholangitis or pancreatitis.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old man comes to a suburban general practice with 16 hours of abdominal pain. It started overnight as a vague ache around his umbilicus and has since moved to the right lower abdomen. He has vomited twice, has not eaten since yesterday, and says the walk from the car park jolted the pain. He has no diarrhoea and no urinary symptoms. He has no past medical history and takes no regular medicines. His temperature is 38.1 °C, heart rate 106/min, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He lies still on the couch. He is tender at McBurney's point with guarding, and pressing on the left iliac fossa causes pain on the right. Bowel sounds are present. A urine dipstick shows ketones 1+ and is negative for blood, leucocytes and nitrites. He asks if he can go home and see how he feels tomorrow.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Arrange an outpatient abdominal ultrasound and review the result tomorrow
Start oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and review him in 24 hours
Withhold all analgesia until a surgeon has examined his abdomen
Give analgesia, keep nil by mouth and arrange same-day hospital referral
Request faecal calprotectin and refer him to a gastroenterologist
questions.explanation: This young man most likely has acute appendicitis. He has periumbilical pain that has moved to the right iliac fossa, anorexia, vomiting, fever, tachycardia, pain when jolted, guarding at McBurney's point and a positive Rovsing's sign. A normal urine dipstick does not rule it out. When appendicitis is suspected in general practice, he needs same-day transfer to an emergency department or surgical unit. The GP should phone a handover, keep him nil by mouth in case he needs theatre, give adequate analgesia, record his allergies and arrange safe transport. Giving analgesia does not hide the diagnosis or delay it. If the diagnosis is confirmed, antibiotics are given in hospital under eTG guidance, alongside appendicectomy or, for some patients, supervised non-operative care. Sending him home raises the risk of perforation, peritonitis and abscess.
why: An outpatient scan with review the next day delays surgical assessment in a febrile, tachycardic patient with localised peritonism, and a normal scan would not exclude appendicitis.
Treating suspected appendicitis with oral antibiotics in the community, without imaging or surgical review, can mask a progressing or perforating appendix and does not follow eTG advice.
Withholding pain relief is outdated, because analgesia does not reduce diagnostic accuracy and leaving pain untreated causes avoidable suffering.
Ileocaecal Crohn's disease is unlikely after a 16-hour illness with no diarrhoea, weight loss or bleeding, and an elective gastroenterology referral would miss a surgical emergency.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman comes to her general practitioner because of 6 weeks of yellow eyes, generalised itch, dark urine and pale stools. A smooth, non-tender mass is palpable below the right costal margin. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiography with stent insertion
Endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle biopsy of the mass
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography of the biliary tree
Repeat CA 19-9 and liver function tests in four weeks
questions.explanation: This woman has obstructive jaundice. She has a conjugated, cholestatic picture with ALP and GGT raised far more than ALT, pale stools, dark urine and itch. A tissue diagnosis is not required before resecting a lesion that looks resectable on imaging; biopsy is arranged by the specialist team, for example before neoadjuvant or palliative chemotherapy.
The pancreatic-protocol CT has already shown the cause and the level of obstruction, so MRCP adds delay without changing the need for specialist referral.
Watching and repeating tests delays the only potentially curative treatment, and CA 19-9 trends do not replace imaging and specialist assessment.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after vomiting dark, coffee-ground material three times this morning. She has had black, sticky stools for 3 days. She has knee osteoarthritis and has taken naproxen 500 mg twice daily for 2 months. She also takes aspirin 100 mg daily because of a previous transient ischaemic attack. She does not drink alcohol. Prophylactic antibiotics such as ceftriaxone lower infection and mortality rates in variceal bleeding in cirrhosis, not in non-variceal ulcer bleeding.
Vitamin K reverses warfarin or treats a deficiency-related coagulopathy, and her INR is normal and she takes no vitamin K antagonist.

questions.stem:
A 64-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a painful, swollen right knee that came on suddenly overnight. Two years ago he had an attack in his left big toe that settled on its own. Serum creatinine 245 µmol/L (60–110)
eGFR 23 mL/min/1.73 m² (>90)
Serum urate 0.52 mmol/L (0.20–0.42)
CRP 64 mg/L (<5)
Synovial fluid: white cell count 22 000 ×10^6/L with 80% neutrophils; needle-shaped, negatively birefringent intracellular crystals; Gram stain shows no organisms; culture pending.

Antibiotics are not indicated when the patient is afebrile, the Gram stain is negative, the synovial count is below 50 000 and urate crystals are present.

Colchicine is cleared by the kidneys and builds up in severe chronic kidney disease, causing toxicity such as diarrhoea, myopathy and bone marrow suppression, so a corticosteroid is the safer choice.
An NSAID given with an angiotensin receptor blocker and a diuretic (the 'triple whammy') in someone with an eGFR of 23 risks acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia.

Empirical antibiotics for septic arthritis are not needed: he is afebrile, the Gram stain is negative, the synovial white cell count is below 50 000 and urate crystals are present, though the culture should still be followed up.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man has 4 months of thirst and nocturia. BMI is 36 kg/m2 with acanthosis nigricans. Urine dipstick shows glucose 3+, ketones negative, specific gravity 1.022.
questions.ask: Which test best confirms the diagnosis?

A water deprivation test looks for diabetes insipidus, which gives dilute urine without glucose, not concentrated urine with glucosuria.
GAD antibodies help tell autoimmune from type 2 diabetes once diabetes is confirmed, but they do not diagnose diabetes itself.
C-peptide measures how much insulin the body still makes, which helps classify diabetes after diagnosis, but it does not confirm hyperglycaemia.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with 3 days of right upper quadrant pain, fever with rigors and yellow eyes. Today his wife noticed he was muddled. He has untreated gallstones and type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. On arrival he is jaundiced and disoriented to time. Temperature is 39.2 °C, pulse 122/min, blood pressure 84/50 mm Hg, respiratory rate 24/min and SpO2 95% on room air. The right upper quadrant is tender. Results: total bilirubin 104 µmol/L (reference <20), conjugated bilirubin 82 µmol/L, ALP 438 U/L (30–110), GGT 590 U/L (<50), ALT 112 U/L (<40), lipase 52 U/L (<60), white cell count 19.1 x10^9/L (4.0–11.0), creatinine 139 µmol/L (60–110), INR 1.2 and venous lactate 3.8 mmol/L (<2.0). Ultrasound shows gallbladder calculi with a 3 mm wall and a common bile duct of 12 mm containing a distal shadowing calculus. Blood cultures are taken, and he is given IV amoxicillin, IV gentamicin and 30 mL/kg of crystalloid. His blood pressure is now 98/60 mm Hg.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: This man has Reynolds' pentad: jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, fever, confusion and hypotension. Under the Tokyo Guidelines 2018 this is severe (grade III) acute cholangitis, because he has neurological and cardiovascular dysfunction. It is caused by a stone in a dilated common bile duct, with a cholestatic liver test pattern, and he also has sepsis with hypoperfusion (lactate 3.8 mmol/L and acute kidney injury). The eTG and the ACSQHC Sepsis Clinical Care Standard say to take blood cultures, give IV antibiotics within 60 minutes (amoxicillin plus gentamicin for biliary sepsis) and give fluids, all of which has been done. Antibiotics alone cannot clear pus from a blocked duct. Once he has been resuscitated, he needs urgent source control by decompressing the bile duct with ERCP (sphincterotomy and stone extraction, or a stent if he is too unstable), and his care should be escalated to ICU. Cholecystectomy should follow once he has recovered, ideally during the same admission. A normal lipase and a thin gallbladder wall make gallstone pancreatitis and acute cholecystitis unlikely.
why: Wrong: cholecystectomy removes the gallbladder but does not clear the stone blocking the common bile duct, and operating on a septic, hypotensive patient is high risk. It is planned after the duct has been cleared and he has recovered.
Wrong: ultrasound has already shown a dilated duct with a stone in it, so MRCP would only delay drainage in a deteriorating septic patient.

Wrong: cholecystostomy drains the gallbladder, not the blocked common bile duct. It is used for acute cholecystitis in unfit patients, whereas percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage is the fallback if ERCP fails.
Wrong: delaying drainage by 72 hours is acceptable only in mild cholangitis that responds to antibiotics. In severe cholangitis with hypotension and confusion, this delay increases the risk of death.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old retired electrician is reviewed on day 3 of admission to the general surgical ward. He came in with 2 days of constant left iliac fossa pain, loose stools and a temperature of 38.4 °C. On admission, CT abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast showed multiple sigmoid diverticula and a 5 cm segment of sigmoid wall thickening with pericolic fat stranding. There was no abscess, extraluminal gas, fistula or obstruction. He was treated with intravenous antibiotics, fluids and paracetamol. He is now afebrile, eating normally and has minimal pain, and he has been switched to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate. He has hypertension treated with perindopril. He has never had any lower bowel investigation and did not return his last two national bowel screening kits. There is no family history of bowel disease. Temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse 72/min and blood pressure 130/80 mm Hg. His abdomen is soft, with mild left iliac fossa tenderness and no guarding. Haemoglobin is 141 g/L (130–180), white cell count 9.2 x10^9/L (4.0–11.0) and CRP 34 mg/L (<5). He is to be discharged today.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate follow-up investigation?
options: CT abdomen and pelvis in 48 hours
questions.explanation: This man has CT-confirmed acute uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis and is getting better on treatment. CT cannot reliably tell inflamed diverticular wall thickening from a sigmoid carcinoma. He is 67, has never had his colon examined and has not done his bowel screening, so cancer in the thickened segment has to be excluded. Colonoscopy should be done once the inflammation has settled, usually about 6 weeks after recovery. CT colonography or flexible sigmoidoscopy are alternatives if colonoscopy is unsuitable. Scoping during acute inflammation is avoided because inflating the bowel with air and passing the scope through the inflamed segment risks perforation. A repeat CT is only needed if he fails to improve within 48 to 72 hours or gets worse. Tumour markers such as CEA are not used to diagnose or screen for colorectal cancer. A faecal immunochemical test is a screening tool for people without symptoms. It cannot replace looking directly at a segment that CT has already shown to be abnormal.
why: A repeat CT is only indicated if he does not improve within 48 to 72 hours or gets worse, and he is clearly improving.
Colonoscopy during or just after acute diverticulitis risks perforating the inflamed colon and is harder to interpret while the inflammation persists, so it should be delayed.
CEA is not sensitive or specific enough to diagnose or exclude colorectal cancer and is used only to monitor known disease.
A faecal immunochemical test is a screening test for people without symptoms and cannot exclude cancer in a sigmoid segment that CT has already shown to be abnormal.

questions.stem:
A 29-year-old woman who is a primary school teacher comes to her general practitioner with a 5-month history of crampy lower abdominal pain and loose stools. She opens her bowels three to four times a day, mostly in the morning, with urgency, and the pain eases after defecation. She is bloated most afternoons. She has had no rectal bleeding or weight loss, and she does not wake at night to open her bowels. She has not travelled overseas. No family members have bowel disease. She takes no regular medicines. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse 76/min, blood pressure 114/70 mm Hg and BMI 23 kg/m2. The abdomen is soft, with mild left iliac fossa tenderness and no masses. Rectal examination is normal. Investigations show:
Haemoglobin 131 g/L (115–165)
Ferritin 62 µg/L (30–300)
C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (<5)
Total IgA 2.0 g/L (0.7–4.0)
Tissue transglutaminase IgA 1 U/mL (<7)
Stool microscopy, culture and PCR: no pathogens detected
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.explanation: This young woman has symptoms that fit irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhoea. She has recurrent lower abdominal pain that eases after defecation, a change in stool frequency and form, and bloating. She has no red flags: no rectal bleeding, weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, anaemia, fever, mass or family history. Her full blood count, ferritin and CRP are normal. Coeliac serology is negative and valid, because her total IgA is normal. Stool tests show no infection. The main serious condition left to exclude is inflammatory bowel disease, because loose stools with urgency in a young adult can be early Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis, and a normal CRP does not rule it out. The first-line test before making a positive diagnosis of IBS is faecal calprotectin, as recommended in eTG and Australian gastroenterology practice. It is cheap and non-invasive. A result below 50 µg/g makes IBD unlikely and avoids colonoscopy. A raised result calls for gastroenterology referral and colonoscopy. Colonoscopy is wrong at this stage because it is invasive and kept for red flags or a raised calprotectin. Duodenal biopsy is wrong because a negative tTG-IgA with normal total IgA makes coeliac disease very unlikely. A lactose hydrogen breath test is wrong because it does not exclude IBD, and a trial of cutting out dairy is the preferred first step. A faecal immunochemical test is wrong because in Australia it is a screening test for people aged 45 to 74 without symptoms, not a way to assess a symptomatic young adult.
why: Colonoscopy is invasive and kept for red flags or a raised calprotectin, neither of which she has yet.
Duodenal biopsy is not needed because a negative tTG-IgA with a normal total IgA makes coeliac disease very unlikely.
A lactose hydrogen breath test cannot exclude inflammatory bowel disease, and a trial of avoiding dairy is preferred over formal breath testing.
A faecal immunochemical test is a population screening tool for people aged 45 to 74 without symptoms and is not used to investigate symptomatic young adults in Australia.
