questions.stem: A 46-year-old man comes to his general practitioner with 3 weeks of sharp anal pain. It starts with each bowel motion and lasts about 2 hours afterwards, and there is a small amount of bright red blood on the toilet paper. The pain began after a week of hard stools while he was driving long-haul freight. For the past 2 weeks he has taken psyllium daily, increased his fluid intake, used warm sitz baths and applied lidocaine gel. His stools are now soft, but the pain has improved only slightly. He has hypertension treated with perindopril and erectile dysfunction treated with tadalafil 5 mg daily. Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 84/min and blood pressure 134/82 mmHg. With a chaperone present, inspection shows a single linear tear in the posterior midline of the anal margin with clean, soft edges. There is no sentinel tag, induration or swelling. He is too tender for a digital rectal examination, so it is not done.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Glyceryl trinitrate 0.2% applied to the anal margin
Diltiazem 2% applied to the anal margin
Hydrocortisone with cinchocaine applied to the anal margin
Botulinum toxin injected into the internal sphincter
questions.explanation: This man has an acute primary anal fissure. The fissure is in the posterior midline, has soft edges and no sentinel tag, and has been present for less than 6 weeks. The pain causes spasm of the internal anal sphincter, which reduces blood flow to the posterior anoderm and stops the tear healing. His stools are now soft, but he is still in pain after 2 weeks of conservative care, so the eTG recommends adding a topical drug that relaxes the sphincter. The two choices are glyceryl trinitrate 0.2% and diltiazem 2%. GTN is contraindicated in anyone taking a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor. He takes tadalafil daily, and its long half-life means simply skipping doses would not make GTN safe. Topical diltiazem 2% twice daily for 6 to 8 weeks heals about as many fissures as GTN and causes fewer headaches. He should keep using fibre, fluids and sitz baths. If the fissure becomes chronic, he should be referred to a surgeon. Any bleeding that continues after the fissure heals needs investigation.
why: GTN with a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor such as daily tadalafil can cause severe, possibly fatal hypotension, so it is contraindicated for him.
Codeine causes constipation, and hard stools would reopen the fissure and keep the pain and spasm going, so it should be avoided.
A topical corticosteroid with local anaesthetic does not relax the sphincter and does not speed fissure healing, and long-term use thins the perianal skin.

Botulinum toxin is a specialist second-line treatment for chronic fissures, or for fissures that have not responded to topical sphincter relaxants, so it is not the next step for an acute fissure that has not yet been treated with one.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance 1 hour after sudden, severe, tearing chest pain that radiated between her shoulder blades while she was gardening. She fainted briefly when the pain began. She has hypertension and smokes 20 cigarettes a day. Her medicines are perindopril and amlodipine. On arrival, her blood pressure is 168/94 mmHg in the left arm and 136/80 mmHg in the right arm, pulse is 104/min and SpO2 is 96% on room air. An early diastolic murmur is heard at the right sternal edge. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia with left ventricular hypertrophy and no ST elevation. CT angiography shows an intimal flap that starts just above the aortic valve and extends into the descending thoracic aorta, with a moderate high-attenuation pericardial effusion. Twenty minutes later she becomes pale and confused. Her blood pressure is 82/54 mmHg, pulse is 124/min, jugular venous pressure is raised 6 cm and her heart sounds are muffled. Two large-bore cannulas are in place and crossmatched blood is available.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Immediate open repair in the operating theatre
questions.explanation: This woman has an acute Stanford type A aortic dissection, because the flap starts in the ascending aorta. She now has the complication most likely to kill her: cardiac tamponade from bleeding into the pericardium. The high-attenuation (blood-density) pericardial effusion, low blood pressure, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds and confusion are the Beck triad with shock. Type A dissection is a surgical emergency. When it is complicated by haemopericardium and shock, the 2024 ESC guidelines and the Heart Foundation/CSANZ guidance used in Australia say she should go straight to theatre for open replacement of the ascending aorta, with blood products given while she is moved. Draining the pericardium only fixes the tamponade, and the blood pressure it restores can make the aorta bleed again. Lowering the heart rate or blood pressure is wrong while she is hypotensive. Anticoagulants make the bleeding worse.
why: Metoprolol is the anti-impulse drug used for a dissection with high blood pressure, but in tamponade and shock it removes the compensating tachycardia and can cause cardiac arrest.

Percutaneous pericardiocentesis raises the blood pressure, which can restart bleeding from the aorta into the pericardium, so it is kept for controlled, small-volume drainage only when theatre cannot be reached in time.
Endovascular stent-graft repair is used for complicated type B (descending) dissection and cannot treat a tear in the ascending aorta just above the valve that is bleeding into the pericardium.
Heparin speeds up bleeding into the pericardium and the false lumen; giving antithrombotics because of the low-grade suspicion of a coronary syndrome is a known harmful error in dissection.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man walks into his general practice without an appointment. He has had chest discomfort for 40 minutes. It began while he was gardening and has not eased with rest. He describes a heavy band across his chest that spreads to his neck and both shoulders, and he feels nauseated and clammy. For the past 2 weeks he has had similar but brief tightness when walking uphill, which settled within minutes of stopping. He has type 2 diabetes and hypertension, and takes metformin and perindopril. He smoked for 35 years and stopped 2 years ago. He is pale and sweaty. Temperature is 36.6°C, pulse 92/min and regular, blood pressure 148/86 mmHg in both arms, respiratory rate 20/min and SpO2 97% on room air. The heart sounds are dual with no murmur, and the chest is clear. Both calves are soft and non-tender.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.explanation: This man has ongoing ischaemic-type chest pain at rest. The pain is heavy, spreads to the neck and shoulders, and comes with nausea and sweating. It follows 2 weeks of new exertional angina, and he has several risk factors: diabetes, hypertension and a long smoking history. This is a possible acute coronary syndrome. Australian guidelines (National Heart Foundation/CSANZ ACS guidelines, eTG Cardiovascular, and the ACSQHC Acute Coronary Syndromes Clinical Care Standard) say a 12-lead ECG should be recorded and read within 10 minutes of first medical contact. It is the single test that sorts the patient into the right pathway straight away. New ST elevation in two or more contiguous leads (or LBBB with ongoing symptoms) means STEMI. In that case, call 000 for ambulance transfer for primary PCI or fibrinolysis, and do not wait for any blood result. If the ECG does not show STEMI, the patient still needs urgent transfer for serial troponins. Equal arm pressures, no aortic regurgitation murmur, normal oxygen saturation and normal calves make aortic dissection and PE less likely, so the ECG comes first. Troponin takes time to rise, and a negative early result cannot rule out infarction, so it must not delay reperfusion. A chest radiograph does not diagnose acute coronary syndrome and would hold up transfer. A D-dimer is used for low-risk suspected PE, and this history does not suggest PE. CT coronary angiography is for stable, low-to-intermediate-risk chest pain, not for ongoing pain at rest.
why: Troponin may still be normal early in infarction and must never delay reperfusion, so it comes after the ECG and should not hold up transfer.
A chest radiograph does not diagnose acute coronary syndrome and would delay the test that decides immediate management.
A D-dimer is used for low-risk suspected pulmonary embolism, and this man has ischaemic-type pain with no PE risk factors, normal SpO2 and normal calves.
CT coronary angiography is for stable, low-to-intermediate-risk chest pain and is not appropriate for ongoing ischaemic pain at rest.

Over the past year her periods have lengthened to 7 days. On heavy days she changes a super pad every 2 hours, floods overnight and passes large clots. She has no bruising, nosebleeds or change in bowel habit. She and her partner stopped using condoms 2 months ago and hope to conceive within the next year. Her only medicine is folic acid 0.5 mg daily. Her blood pressure is 114/72 mmHg, pulse 98/min and temperature 36.7 °C. She has conjunctival pallor. Abdominal, speculum and bimanual examinations are normal. Investigations show:
Haemoglobin 92 g/L (115–165)
MCV 71 fL (80–100)
Platelets 438 x10^9/L (150–400)
Ferritin 5 µg/L (30–300)
CRP 3 mg/L (<5)
TSH 1.9 mIU/L (0.4–4.0)
Urine β-hCG negative
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Oral iron and a levonorgestrel intrauterine device
Oral iron and the combined oral contraceptive pill
Intravenous iron and tranexamic acid during menses
Oral iron and tranexamic acid during menses
Oral iron and referral for diagnostic hysteroscopy
questions.explanation: She has iron deficiency anaemia (Hb 92 g/L, MCV 71 fL, reactive thrombocytosis, ferritin 5 µg/L with a normal CRP) caused by heavy menstrual bleeding. Management must replace the deficit and treat the cause. Under eTG and the National Blood Authority guidance, oral iron is first line in a stable patient who has not yet tried it. Daily or alternate-day dosing works, and alternate-day dosing may improve absorption and tolerance. Recheck the FBC in 2 to 4 weeks (expect a rise of about 20 g/L by 3 to 4 weeks) and continue for about 3 months after the Hb normalises. The levonorgestrel IUD is usually first line for heavy menstrual bleeding (ACSQHC Clinical Care Standard), but it and the combined pill both prevent pregnancy, and she is trying to conceive. Tranexamic acid (1 g orally three to four times daily for up to 5 days during heavy bleeding) is a non-hormonal option. It reduces menstrual loss by about 40 to 50%, is taken only while bleeding and does not affect fertility. She has a normal pelvic examination and no risk factors for endometrial pathology, so invasive investigation is not needed yet. B: the LNG-IUD is contraceptive and does not suit a woman trying to conceive. C: the combined pill prevents ovulation and conception, so it goes against her plan for pregnancy. D: IV iron is for oral intolerance, failure, malabsorption or a need for rapid repletion, and none of these applies. E: hysteroscopy is for women aged 45 or older, those with risk factors for endometrial hyperplasia or cancer, or those whose medical treatment has failed.
why: Wrong: the levonorgestrel IUD is contraceptive, so it conflicts with her wish to conceive, even though it is often first line for heavy menstrual bleeding.
Wrong: the combined oral contraceptive pill suppresses ovulation and prevents the pregnancy she is trying for.
Wrong: intravenous iron is reserved for oral intolerance, failure, malabsorption or a need for rapid repletion, and she is stable and has not tried oral iron.
Wrong: hysteroscopy is not indicated in a 24-year-old with a normal pelvic examination, no endometrial risk factors and no failed medical treatment.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman comes to a rural emergency department with a racing heart and mild central chest tightness. Both started suddenly 70 minutes ago while she was watching television. She has never had this before. She has hypertension treated with perindopril and type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. Her pulse is 138/min and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 132/84 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air and temperature 36.7 °C. Her chest is clear and she has no peripheral oedema. A 12-lead ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of about 140/min, a narrow QRS and no ST-segment or T-wave change. Blood was taken on arrival, 75 minutes after symptom onset: high-sensitivity troponin T 9 ng/L (99th centile 14), creatinine 84 µmol/L (eGFR 66 mL/min/1.73 m^2), potassium 4.4 mmol/L and TSH 2.1 mIU/L (reference 0.4 to 4.0).
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of her troponin result?
options: Myocardial infarction cannot yet be ruled out at this point
Acute myocardial infarction is excluded by this single value
Rate-related type 2 myocardial infarction is confirmed
Chronic myocardial injury from renal impairment is shown
Unstable angina is excluded by this normal value
questions.explanation: Her high-sensitivity troponin T of 9 ng/L is below the 99th centile, but it was taken only 75 minutes after her symptoms began. Troponin takes time to rise after myocardial injury, so one value taken this soon can miss an evolving infarction. The NHFA/CSANZ ACS guideline accepts a single-sample rule-out only when the hs-troponin T is very low (below about 5 ng/L) and symptoms started more than 3 hours before the sample. Otherwise, the test is repeated using an accelerated protocol (usually at 2 hours, or at 1 hour with validated algorithms) and the change between the two values is assessed. Her chest tightness, age, hypertension and diabetes make ACS an important alternative cause and a possible trigger for her AF. So this result does not yet rule out myocardial infarction, and she needs a repeat troponin while her AF is rate-controlled. A: A value below the 99th centile does not rule out infarction when it is taken less than 3 hours after onset and is above the very-low threshold. C: A type 2 infarction needs troponin above the 99th centile with a rise or fall, and her value is normal. D: Chronic myocardial injury means a stable troponin above the 99th centile, and her eGFR of 66 does not explain any rise. E: Troponin is normal in unstable angina by definition, so a normal value cannot exclude it.
why: Correct: a single hs-troponin T below the 99th centile but above the very-low rule-out level, taken under 3 hours after onset, cannot rule out infarction, so a repeat is needed.
Wrong: a type 2 infarction needs troponin above the 99th centile with a rise or fall, and her value is normal.
Wrong: chronic myocardial injury means a stable troponin above the 99th centile, and her near-normal renal function does not explain any rise.
Wrong: troponin is normal in unstable angina by definition, so a normal value cannot exclude it.

questions.stem:
A 74-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 2 days of colicky abdominal pain, distension and repeated vomiting, which is now faeculent. She has passed no flatus for 24 hours. She has known gallstones and has never had abdominal surgery. Her medicines are perindopril, metformin and ibuprofen. Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse is 108/min, blood pressure is 112/68 mmHg and respiratory rate is 16/min. Her mucous membranes are dry. Her abdomen is distended, with high-pitched bowel sounds and no peritonism. An abdominal X-ray shows dilated small bowel loops with multiple air-fluid levels. Venous blood results:
pH 7.43 (7.32 to 7.42)
pCO2 46 mmHg (41 to 51)
Bicarbonate 30 mmol/L (22 to 28)
Base excess +6 mmol/L (-2 to +2)
Lactate 1.8 mmol/L (less than 2.0)
Sodium 136 mmol/L (135 to 145)
Potassium 2.8 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2)
Chloride 93 mmol/L (95 to 110)
Creatinine 128 µmol/L (her baseline is 78)
questions.ask: Which of the following best describes these blood gas findings?
options: Respiratory acidosis with renal bicarbonate retention
Lactic acidosis from metformin and kidney injury
Normal anion gap acidosis from small bowel losses
Metabolic alkalosis from gastric acid and volume loss
Mixed high anion gap acidosis and alkalosis
questions.explanation: The pH is at the alkalaemic end, and bicarbonate (30 mmol/L) and base excess (+6) are both raised. That means the main problem is metabolic alkalosis. The low chloride (93 mmol/L) and low potassium (2.8 mmol/L) show it is hypochloraemic and hypokalaemic, the typical picture with vomiting. Losing gastric hydrochloric acid produces the alkalosis. Losing volume then keeps it going: it causes a prerenal acute kidney injury (creatinine 1.6 times her baseline) and switches on aldosterone, so the kidney holds on to bicarbonate and loses potassium. A venous pCO2 of 46 mmHg is within the normal range and fits mild respiratory compensation, not a primary respiratory problem. The anion gap is normal (136 - (93 + 30) = 13) and lactate is normal, so there is no hidden acidosis, although a normal lactate does not rule out bowel ischaemia. In practice she needs IV 0.9% sodium chloride with potassium chloride, magnesium checked, and her perindopril, metformin and ibuprofen withheld.
why: Wrong: a primary respiratory acidosis needs an acidaemic pH and a raised pCO2, but her pH is high and her venous pCO2 is normal, so the raised bicarbonate is the primary change.
Wrong: metformin and the kidney injury make this a tempting choice, but her lactate (1.8 mmol/L), anion gap (13) and pH are all normal, so there is no lactic acidosis.
Wrong: losing alkaline small bowel fluid can cause a normal anion gap acidosis, but her bicarbonate is raised and her pH is not acidaemic.
Wrong: with a normal anion gap of 13 and a normal lactate, there is no evidence of a second, high anion gap acidosis alongside the alkalosis.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 3 days of tingling that started in her feet and has spread up to her waist. Over the same time her legs have become steadily weaker. Since this morning she has been unable to pass urine. She has had no back pain, fever, trauma or weight loss. Eighteen months ago she had 2 weeks of blurred vision and pain on moving her left eye, which got better without treatment. She takes no medicines. Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 80 beats/min, blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg and respiratory rate 16 breaths/min. Cranial nerve and upper limb examination is normal. Tone is increased in both legs. Hip flexion and ankle dorsiflexion are 3/5 on the left and 4/5 on the right. Knee and ankle reflexes are brisk, and both plantar responses are extensor. Pinprick sensation is reduced below the umbilicus. A bladder scan shows 900 mL. Full blood count and C-reactive protein are normal.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Lumbar puncture for CSF oligoclonal bands
Nerve conduction studies of both lower limbs
Urgent MRI of the lumbosacral spine only
Urgent gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the whole spine
questions.explanation: Both legs are weak with spastic tone, brisk reflexes and extensor plantars, so this is an upper motor neuron lesion. The arms and cranial nerves are normal, and there is a sensory level at the umbilicus (T10) with urinary retention, so the lesion is in the thoracic spinal cord. An acute myelopathy with a sensory level and loss of bladder control is cord compression until proven otherwise. The next step is an urgent MRI of the whole spine with gadolinium. Imaging the whole spine matters because a sensory level only gives the lowest possible level of the lesion, and there can be lesions at more than one level. The same scan separates a compressive cause (disc, tumour, abscess, haematoma) from an inflammatory myelitis. Her past episode of painful vision loss suggests optic neuritis, so this may be a second demyelinating attack (multiple sclerosis). A brain MRI is usually done at the same time. CSF and antibody tests come after imaging has ruled out compression.
why: CSF oligoclonal bands help confirm multiple sclerosis, but a lumbar puncture should not be done before imaging has ruled out cord compression, and it would delay the time-critical scan.

Nerve conduction studies look for a peripheral process such as Guillain-Barré syndrome, which causes floppy weakness with absent reflexes, not spastic weakness with brisk reflexes, extensor plantars and a truncal sensory level.
A lumbosacral scan only looks at the cauda equina and would miss the thoracic cord lesion suggested by upper motor neuron signs and a T10 sensory level.
Aquaporin-4 antibodies help tell neuromyelitis optica from multiple sclerosis, but the result takes days and does not rule out cord compression, so it is not the next investigation.

questions.stem: A 20-hour-old girl is reviewed on the postnatal ward because the midwife reports that she has stopped feeding and started grunting. She was born vaginally at 39+2 weeks, weighing 3.4 kg, with Apgar scores of 8 and 9. She fed well for the first 12 hours. Her mother carried group B streptococcus and received intravenous benzylpenicillin 90 minutes before the birth. The membranes had ruptured 22 hours before delivery, and the mother's temperature in labour was 38.4 °C. On examination, the baby is lethargic and mottled. Temperature is 38.3 °C, pulse 184/min, respirations 72/min, systolic pressure 55 mmHg and oxygen saturation 92% on room air. Capillary refill time is 4 seconds. She has subcostal recession and grunting. Heart sounds are normal and the femoral pulses are palpable. Capillary glucose is 3.9 mmol/L. Intravenous access has been obtained, and antibiotics are about to be given.
questions.ask: Which of the following investigations is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This term baby has early-onset neonatal sepsis with shock. She has a fever, tachycardia, tachypnoea, grunting, a capillary refill time of 4 seconds, mottling and lethargy. She also has four risk factors: maternal GBS carriage, intrapartum antibiotics given less than 4 hours before birth, membranes ruptured for 18 hours or more, and maternal fever in labour. A positive blood culture is the reference standard for confirming early-onset sepsis. It identifies the organism (most often GBS or E. coli) and its antibiotic sensitivities. Under the RCH Neonatal antimicrobial guidelines and Queensland Clinical Guidelines, at least 1 mL is taken before the first doses of benzylpenicillin and gentamicin, but antibiotics are not delayed to get it. The culture result and the baby's condition are then used to review antibiotics at 36 hours. CRP and procalcitonin are nonspecific markers that can support the diagnosis but cannot confirm it. Urine culture has little value in early-onset sepsis. A chest X-ray shows lung involvement but does not show what organism is causing it.
why: CRP takes 12 to 24 hours to rise and can be raised by non-infectious causes, so it helps to monitor or rule out infection but cannot confirm sepsis.
Procalcitonin rises normally in the first 48 hours of life, and it is not a confirmatory test in Australian neonatal sepsis guidelines.
Early-onset sepsis comes from maternal flora at birth, not from the urinary tract, so urine culture is not recommended in the first 72 hours and would rarely be positive.
A chest X-ray may show pneumonia, but GBS pneumonia can look the same as surfactant deficiency or transient tachypnoea, and the film cannot identify an organism.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman who works as a hairdresser sees her general practitioner with 10 weeks of right neck pain. The pain runs down the back of her arm to her middle finger and is worse when she looks up. Eight weeks ago she started regular paracetamol and ibuprofen and a supervised physiotherapy program. The pain has eased only a little, and she still drops her hair dryer. She has no hand clumsiness, change in gait or bladder symptoms. She has hypertension treated with amlodipine. Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 74/min and regular, and blood pressure 134/80 mmHg. Right elbow extension and wrist flexion are 4-/5, the same as 8 weeks ago, and the right triceps reflex is reduced. Sensation is reduced over the right middle finger. Tone, coordination and the lower limb examination are normal, and Hoffmann's sign is absent. MRI of the neck shows severe right C6-7 foraminal stenosis compressing the right C7 nerve root, with a normal cord.

options: Same-day transfer to an emergency department
Outpatient referral to a spine surgeon
questions.explanation: This is a right C7 radiculopathy from cervical spondylosis. The radicular pain runs to the middle finger and gets worse on neck extension. There is weakness of elbow extension and wrist flexion, a reduced triceps reflex and C7 sensory loss, and the MRI shows concordant C6-7 foraminal stenosis. Most cervical radiculopathy settles with analgesia, physiotherapy and modified activity. This patient has had 8 weeks of conservative treatment and still has an objective motor deficit, a matching MRI lesion and pain that limits her work. Urgent assessment is not needed: there are no myelopathic symptoms, no upper motor neuron signs, her weakness is not getting worse and the cord is normal. She still needs safety netting to seek urgent review if weakness progresses, or if hand clumsiness, gait disturbance or bladder symptoms develop. Continuing physiotherapy alone delays treatment of a persisting motor deficit. Transfer to the emergency department is for myelopathy or rapidly progressive weakness. Carotid imaging investigates a TIA, which this fixed lower motor neuron deficit with radicular pain is not. A rigid collar long term is not recommended and causes stiffness and deconditioning.

Same-day emergency transfer is for suspected cord compression, myelopathy or rapidly progressive weakness, and she has none of these: there are no upper motor neuron signs, the cord is normal and her deficit is stable.
Carotid duplex ultrasonography is part of the workup for a TIA, but she has a fixed lower motor neuron deficit in one root pattern with radicular pain, not transient episodes of focal weakness.
Immobilising the neck in a rigid collar for weeks has no proven benefit in cervical radiculopathy and causes stiffness and muscle deconditioning.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman is admitted from the emergency department of a regional hospital. She has had 2 days of colicky periumbilical pain and bilious vomiting, and she has passed no flatus. She has had two caesarean sections and an open appendicectomy. Adhesive small bowel obstruction is diagnosed. She is treated with nil by mouth, nasogastric decompression and intravenous fluids with added potassium. Eight hours later her pain is constant and severe despite intravenous morphine. Temperature is 38.1°C, pulse 126/min, blood pressure 104/66 mm Hg and respirations 22/min. The abdomen is distended, with localised tenderness and guarding in the right lower quadrant, and bowel sounds are reduced. Nasogastric output so far is 1.4 L. Leukocyte count is 16.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0). Venous lactate is 1.5 mmol/L (less than 2.0). CT of the abdomen with intravenous contrast shows a closed loop of small bowel with reduced wall enhancement and fluid in the mesentery.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: The most serious risk in adhesive small bowel obstruction is strangulation, where the bowel loses its blood supply and dies. This patient has the warning signs. Her pain has changed from colicky to constant and is not controlled by morphine. She has a fever, a rising heart rate, localised guarding and a raised white cell count. CT shows a closed loop with reduced wall enhancement and fluid in the mesentery. The WSES Bologna guidelines say that strangulation, a closed loop, peritonitis or ischaemia on CT are reasons to stop non-operative management and operate straight away. This lets the surgeon release the bowel and remove any dead segment before it perforates and causes sepsis. Lactate often rises only once bowel has already died, so a normal value does not exclude ischaemia and should not delay the operation. In a regional hospital this means calling the surgeon now and, if no one there can operate, arranging urgent transfer. Resuscitation and antibiotics should continue while this happens.
why: A water-soluble contrast challenge is used to predict which uncomplicated obstructions will settle without an operation, and it is not appropriate when CT shows strangulation.
Lactate rises late in bowel ischaemia, so waiting for a repeat value delays the operation while more bowel dies.
Conservative management for up to 72 hours is only for uncomplicated adhesive obstruction without signs of ischaemia, and continuing it here risks perforation.
Colonoscopic decompression treats large bowel problems such as sigmoid volvulus or pseudo-obstruction and cannot reach or relieve an obstructed small bowel loop.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman presents to the emergency department 2 days after a day-surgery hysteroscopy and dilatation and curettage for heavy, irregular bleeding. Since yesterday evening she has had worsening lower abdominal pain, nausea and anorexia. The operation record describes a retroverted, bulky uterus and a view partly obscured by blood, and lists the procedure as uneventful. The histology report, released this morning, describes disordered proliferative endometrium with fragments of mature adipose tissue. She has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin, and her body mass index is 42 kg/m2. Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse 104/min, blood pressure 132/80 mm Hg, respiratory rate 20/min and SpO2 97% on room air. The lower abdomen is tender with voluntary guarding but no rigidity, and bowel sounds are reduced. There is scant brown vaginal loss. White cell count is 15.6 x 10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C-reactive protein 148 mg/L (less than 5) and lactate 1.6 mmol/L (less than 2.0). Fluids, analgesia and antibiotics have been started.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast
MRI of the pelvis with gadolinium
questions.explanation: There should be no fat inside the uterus. Adipose tissue in the curettings means the curette went through the uterine wall into omentum, mesentery or bowel fat, so this is uterine perforation until proven otherwise. A perforation like this can injure bowel without anyone noticing, and the injury often shows itself days later. That fits this patient: fever, lower abdominal guarding, reduced bowel sounds and high inflammatory markers 2 days after surgery. She is haemodynamically stable, her lactate is normal and she has no generalised peritonitis, so there is time to image her before deciding on surgery. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis is the best test here. It can show free fluid, free gas, a collection or abscess, bowel wall thickening or a leak, and bleeding, and it is not limited by her body habitus. A senior gynaecologist and the general surgeons should be told now. If the CT shows a visceral injury, or if she deteriorates, she needs laparoscopy or laparotomy. Erect chest X-ray: free gas under the diaphragm is not reliable after recent uterine instrumentation, and the film shows nothing about the pelvis, collections or bowel. Transvaginal ultrasound: it may show free fluid or a pelvic collection, but obesity limits the views and it cannot reliably find bowel injury or free gas. MRI of the pelvis: it is slow, less available urgently, covers only the pelvis and is poor at showing free gas and bowel leaks in an acutely unwell patient. CT pulmonary angiography: her tachycardia and fever are explained by an intra-abdominal source, her oxygen saturation is normal and she has no respiratory symptoms.
why: Free gas can enter the peritoneum through a uterine perforation during hysteroscopy, so finding it does not tell you the bowel is injured, and the film cannot show collections or pelvic disease.
With a body mass index of 42 the views are limited, and ultrasound cannot reliably find bowel injury, free gas or collections higher in the abdomen.
MRI is slow and less available as an emergency test, covers only the pelvis and is poor at showing free gas or a bowel leak in a febrile, acutely unwell patient.
She has no chest symptoms and normal oxygen saturation, and her fever, tachycardia and lower abdominal guarding point to an intra-abdominal source rather than pulmonary embolism.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with sudden severe breathlessness that began overnight. For 3 weeks he has needed three pillows to sleep, and his ankles have become swollen. He had an anterior myocardial infarction treated with a stent 9 years ago, and he has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. He has had no cardiac imaging since the infarct. On arrival, pulse is 112/min, blood pressure 178/96 mmHg, respiratory rate 30/min and SpO2 86% on room air. His jugular venous pressure is raised, there is a third heart sound, crackles reach the mid-zones and there is pitting oedema to the shins. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with Q waves in V1 to V4, unchanged from 2 years ago. Chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly, upper lobe diversion, Kerley B lines and small bilateral pleural effusions. NT-proBNP is 5800 ng/L. hs-troponin I is 42 ng/L, and 45 ng/L 3 hours later (99th percentile below 34 ng/L). He improves with non-invasive ventilation, glyceryl trinitrate and IV furosemide.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation to establish the underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This man has acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, which is acute decompensated heart failure. The supporting findings are orthopnoea, leg oedema, a raised JVP, an S3, a chest X-ray showing oedema and effusions, and an NT-proBNP well above the rule-in threshold for his age. His old anterior infarct points to an ischaemic cardiomyopathy. The 2018 NHFA/CSANZ heart failure guideline recommends transthoracic echocardiography for every patient with suspected heart failure. It confirms the structural or functional cardiac cause. It measures LVEF, which separates HFrEF from HFpEF and decides which disease-modifying drugs to use. It also shows regional wall motion abnormalities, valve disease, filling pressures and pulmonary pressures. It is non-invasive and can be done at the bedside once he is stable. The troponin is raised but nearly flat (42 then 45 ng/L) with an unchanged ECG. That pattern fits myocardial injury from heart failure, not an acute MI. Bilateral effusions with pulmonary oedema are expected transudates that settle with diuresis.
why: Coronary angiography is not the next test: the troponin is flat and the ECG is unchanged, so there is no acute coronary syndrome needing urgent invasive assessment, and angiography does not define ventricular function or the type of heart failure.
CT pulmonary angiography is not indicated: heart failure explains the whole picture, the leg swelling is bilateral, and IV contrast adds risk without addressing the likely diagnosis.

Diagnostic pleural aspiration is not needed: small bilateral effusions with pulmonary oedema in heart failure are presumed transudates and are managed with diuresis, with aspiration kept for atypical, unilateral or non-resolving effusions.
Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging is a second-line test, used when echocardiography images are inadequate or a specific cardiomyopathy needs characterising, and it is not the first investigation.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man sees his general practitioner because of 10 weeks of crampy right lower abdominal pain and four to six loose stools a day. options: Phytomenadione 1 mg by slow intravenous injection

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has sudden tearing chest pain through to his back. CT shows an ascending aortic intimal flap. His BP falls to 80/50 mmHg with distended neck veins and pulsus paradoxus.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman sees her general practitioner because she has not opened her bowels for 6 days. Nine days ago she had an uncomplicated laparoscopic appendicectomy. She went home on oxycodone 5 mg up to four times daily, which she still takes three times a day. She was given no bowel medicine. Her last stools were small and hard. She had to strain, passing them caused sharp anal pain, and there was bright red blood on the toilet paper. She is passing flatus and has no vomiting or abdominal pain. She takes ferrous sulfate for iron deficiency. Temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse 78/min and blood pressure 120/78 mm Hg. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender, and bowel sounds are normal. Anal inspection shows a posterior midline fissure. Digital rectal examination finds hard stool and no mass. Haemoglobin is 124 g/L (115–165), ferritin 20 µg/L (30–300), corrected calcium 2.38 mmol/L (2.10–2.60) and TSH 1.4 mIU/L (0.5–4.0). The opioid will be weaned and simple analgesia started.

Postoperative ileus and obstruction are unlikely: she is passing flatus, has no pain or vomiting, and her abdomen is soft with normal bowel sounds. Opioids slow gut transit and make stools dry and hard. eTG recommends a regular stimulant laxative (such as senna) combined with an osmotic laxative (such as macrogol) for opioid-induced constipation, continued while she takes the opioid. Treatment should then be stepped down. Fibre, warm baths and simple analgesia help as well, and topical glyceryl trinitrate or diltiazem can be added if the fissure does not heal. Bulk-forming agents add volume without improving the slowed transit, and can make symptoms worse. Peripherally acting opioid antagonists are used only when standard laxatives have failed. Softeners alone and as-needed rectal treatment are not enough for ongoing opioid use.
why: Bulk-forming laxatives are not recommended in opioid-induced constipation because they add bulk to slowed bowel and can worsen bloating and impaction.
Peripherally acting opioid antagonists are kept for constipation that has not responded to standard laxatives, which she has not yet tried.
A stool softener on its own does not overcome the slowed transit caused by opioids and is not effective enough as the only treatment.
As-needed suppositories are a rescue measure, not maintenance therapy, and inserting them through a painful acute fissure is poorly tolerated.

On arrival she is agitated and can speak only in single words. Temperature is 36.4 °C, pulse 138/min, blood pressure 82/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 34/min, and oxygen saturation 85% on 15 L/min via a non-rebreather mask. Her trachea is deviated to the left and her neck veins are distended. There is bruising and tenderness over the right lateral ribs. The right hemithorax is hyper-resonant to percussion, and breath sounds are absent on the right. Heart sounds are clearly audible. Two large-bore cannulae are in place and blood has been sent for group and hold. A mobile chest X-ray has been requested, and the radiographer will arrive in 10 minutes.

Subxiphoid pericardiocentesis guided by bedside ultrasound
Rapid sequence intubation followed by positive-pressure ventilation
Needle decompression at the fifth intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line
Intravenous bolus of 1 L warmed crystalloid over 15 minutes

A chest X-ray should be done only after that.

Wrong: tamponade is unlikely because her trachea is deviated, one side of her chest is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds, and her heart sounds are clear, so the chest needs decompressing rather than the pericardium.
Wrong: positive-pressure ventilation forces more air into the pleural space and can quickly worsen a tension pneumothorax and cause arrest if the chest has not been decompressed first.
Wrong: her shock is obstructive, not caused by blood loss, so fluid will not restore venous return while the tension pneumothorax is untreated, and giving it delays the treatment that saves her life.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman is reviewed on the medical ward on day 3 of treatment for herpes simplex virus type 1 encephalitis, confirmed by CSF PCR. She has rheumatoid arthritis, and her weekly methotrexate has been withheld since admission. She weighs 70 kg and is receiving aciclovir 10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours. She is still drowsy and has been drinking little. Her maintenance drip was taken down yesterday when the cannula tissued, and it was not restarted. Her urine output over the past 12 hours is 250 mL. Temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse 98/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min and SpO2 97% on room air. Her mucous membranes are dry, and there is no new focal neurological deficit. Serum creatinine is 164 µmol/L (72 µmol/L on admission; reference 45–90), urea 11.8 mmol/L, sodium 140 mmol/L and potassium 4.6 mmol/L. Urine microscopy shows needle-shaped birefringent crystals.

options: Stop the antiviral and start oral valaciclovir 1 g three times daily
Stop the antiviral and start intravenous foscarnet
Continue the current regimen and add intravenous furosemide 40 mg
Arrange urgent haemodialysis through a temporary vascular catheter
Start isotonic crystalloid and reduce antiviral dosing to match renal function
questions.explanation: This patient has acute kidney injury from aciclovir crystal nephropathy. Aciclovir is cleared by the kidneys and is poorly soluble in urine, so high-dose IV therapy in a dehydrated patient lets crystals form in the renal tubules. This is the main complication to prevent during treatment of HSV encephalitis, and it is why eTG advises keeping the patient well hydrated and monitoring renal function throughout. Her intake is poor, her drip has been stopped, she is oliguric with dry mucous membranes, her creatinine has more than doubled and her urine shows needle-shaped birefringent crystals. The right step is to restart isotonic IV fluids and adjust the aciclovir dose to her estimated creatinine clearance. Her Cockcroft-Gault clearance is about 30 mL/min, which calls for 10 mg/kg every 12 hours. IV therapy should continue for the full course, at least 14 to 21 days in an immunosuppressed patient, because stopping or under-treating HSV encephalitis carries high mortality and neurological morbidity. The injury usually reverses with hydration and dose adjustment. Methotrexate should stay withheld, because it is also cleared by the kidneys and would add toxicity.
why: Wrong: oral valaciclovir is not recommended for acute HSV encephalitis while the patient is drowsy and still in the IV phase, and it is converted to aciclovir, so it would not prevent crystal formation.
Wrong: foscarnet is reserved for aciclovir-resistant HSV and is more nephrotoxic, so it would make her kidney injury worse.
Wrong: furosemide would deepen her volume depletion and does nothing to clear crystals, and keeping full-dose aciclovir at this clearance would cause further accumulation and toxicity.
Wrong: she has no indication for urgent dialysis (no hyperkalaemia, acidosis, fluid overload or uraemic complications), and this injury usually reverses with hydration and dose adjustment.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department at 11 pm by his mother with noisy breathing. He has had a runny nose and fever for 2 days, and this evening developed a barking cough and a hoarse cry. He is fully immunised and has no medical history. He weighs 12 kg. On arrival he was agitated, with stridor at rest, marked sternal and subcostal recession, and SpO2 91% in room air. He was given nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 (5 mL undiluted) and oral dexamethasone 7.2 mg (0.6 mg/kg), with oxygen held near his face. Sixty minutes later he is sitting on his mother's lap and playing. Temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse 132/min, respiratory rate 28/min, and SpO2 97% in room air. He has an occasional barking cough, no stridor at rest and no chest wall recession. His mother would like to take him home now because his older sister is home alone with a neighbour.

Obtain a lateral neck X-ray before deciding on discharge
Give a second nebulised adrenaline treatment before discharge
Observe for at least 3 hours after the last adrenaline treatment
Arrange admission to intensive care for elective intubation
questions.explanation: This child had severe croup: stridor at rest, a marked increase in work of breathing, agitation and hypoxaemia. Nebulised adrenaline works within minutes but wears off within about 2 hours. Dexamethasone takes several hours to reach full effect, so the obstruction can come back once the adrenaline wears off. The RCH Croup CPG says to observe for at least 3 hours after the last adrenaline dose. Discharge is appropriate only if there is still no stridor at rest at that point, with clear safety-netting advice. The improvement at 60 minutes is likely the adrenaline effect and is not proof that the illness is settling. A mild tachycardia is expected after adrenaline. Discharging now risks the obstruction returning at home in the middle of the night. A lateral neck X-ray is not needed in typical croup, would not change management and could upset the child. Giving more adrenaline to a child with no stridor at rest has no benefit, and it would only restart the observation period. Wrong: croup is a clinical diagnosis and this course is typical, so imaging would not change management and upsetting the child can worsen obstruction.
Wrong: adrenaline is given for severe obstruction such as stridor at rest with marked work of breathing, and has no preventive role in a child who has none.
Wrong: intubation is kept for a tiring child, ongoing hypoxaemia or repeated adrenaline needs, none of which this improving child has.

questions.stem:
A 19-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance from a general practice. He has had 14 hours of worsening generalised headache, fever and photophobia. Five days ago he came back from a week in a crowded backpacker hostel. The general practitioner gave benzylpenicillin 2.4 g intramuscularly 4 hours ago, before transfer. He takes no medicines, and his vaccination history is unknown. His temperature is 38.8 °C, pulse 116/min, respirations 22/min, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg and SpO2 98% on room air. He is alert and oriented (GCS 15). He has neck stiffness, with no focal neurological signs, papilloedema or rash. Two sets of blood cultures were taken on arrival. Lumbar puncture fluid analysis shows:
Appearance: turbid
Neutrophils: 2900 x10^6/L (reference 0)
Lymphocytes: 40 x10^6/L (reference less than 5)
Protein: 1.3 g/L (reference 0.15 to 0.45)
Glucose: 1.1 mmol/L (paired serum glucose 5.6 mmol/L)
Gram stain: neutrophils seen, no organisms seen
questions.ask: Which of the following investigations is most likely to identify the causative organism?
options: Bacterial culture of the CSF sample
Bacterial PCR on the CSF sample
Repeat blood cultures from two sites
Viral PCR panel on the CSF sample
questions.explanation: This young adult has fever, headache, photophobia and neck stiffness after crowded living. His lumbar puncture fluid shows a marked neutrophil-predominant pleocytosis, high protein and a CSF-to-serum glucose ratio of about 0.2 (below 0.4). These findings mean bacterial meningitis, most likely meningococcal. He correctly had parenteral benzylpenicillin in general practice before transfer. However, that dose sterilises the CSF and blood within hours, which explains why the Gram stain shows no organisms and why culture yield will be low. Nucleic acid testing (PCR) for Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae on the CSF does not need live bacteria. It stays positive for days after antibiotics have started. eTG and the CDNA invasive meningococcal disease guidelines recommend it, and it is the test most likely to confirm the organism (and give the serogroup for public health) in a pretreated patient. Culture of the CSF should still be sent, because it gives antibiotic susceptibilities, but it is less likely to grow anything. Repeat blood cultures taken even later after antibiotics will give an even lower yield. A throat swab shows only nasopharyngeal carriage, so it cannot confirm invasive disease. A viral PCR panel does not fit the bacterial CSF picture.
why: Correct: PCR detects bacterial DNA even after antibiotics have killed the organisms, so it is the most sensitive way to confirm N. meningitidis (and its serogroup) in pretreated meningitis.
Blood cultures taken even longer after the antibiotic dose are less likely to grow anything than the sets already taken on arrival.
A positive throat culture shows only nasopharyngeal carriage, which is common in young adults, so it supports the diagnosis but cannot confirm invasive disease.
A neutrophilic CSF with high protein and a glucose ratio below 0.4 points to a bacterial cause, not a viral one, so a viral panel will not identify this organism.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman comes back to her general practitioner 6 weeks after she was diagnosed with ulcerative colitis. Before the diagnosis she had 10 weeks of bloody, mucousy diarrhoea and left-sided abdominal cramps. Stool pathogen tests were negative. Ileocolonoscopy found continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum to 30 cm and a normal proximal colon and terminal ileum. Biopsies showed crypt distortion with no granulomas and no dysplasia. She now takes oral mesalazine and mesalazine enemas. She has 1 to 2 formed stools a day with no blood. She has never smoked. Her mother was diagnosed with bowel cancer at age 62. No other relatives have had bowel cancer. Temperature is 36.7°C, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg and pulse 72/min. Her abdomen is soft and not tender. Haemoglobin is 129 g/L (115–165), CRP 3 mg/L (<5), ALP 74 U/L (30–110) and GGT 18 U/L (<40). She asks how her bowel cancer risk will be checked.

Faecal immunochemical test every 2 years from age 45
CT colonography every 5 years starting now

Her colitis runs from the rectum to 30 cm, so it is left-sided (Montreal E2) and not proctitis alone. After that, the interval (1, 3 or 5 years) is set by risk factors such as ongoing inflammation, strictures, past dysplasia, PSC and family history. Her mother's cancer at 62 may shorten later intervals, but it does not change the start point. Population or family-history screening does not apply to her, because her colitis is the bigger risk and needs colonoscopy with targeted biopsies. Annual colonoscopy straight away is only for coexisting primary sclerosing cholangitis, and her normal ALP and GGT make this unlikely.

Two-yearly faecal immunochemical tests are average-risk population screening, and they cannot detect flat colitis-associated dysplasia or tell it apart from inflammatory bleeding.
Annual colonoscopy from diagnosis is for patients who also have primary sclerosing cholangitis, and her normal ALP and GGT make this unlikely.
CT colonography cannot take biopsies or show flat dysplasia, so it is not used for surveillance in inflammatory bowel disease.

questions.stem:
A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance with a headache that has got steadily worse over 6 hours. The headache is generalised and throbbing, and he has fever, rigors, vomiting and pain when looking at lights. He has no history of headaches, head injury or seizures, and he takes no medicines. His temperature is 39.3 °C, pulse 118/min, blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg, respiratory rate 22/min and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He is alert and oriented, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Neck flexion is painful and restricted. Fundoscopy shows sharp optic disc margins. Cranial nerve and limb examinations are normal, and there is no rash. Blood cultures are taken, and he is given dexamethasone 10 mg IV and ceftriaxone 2 g IV. Laboratory studies show:
White cell count 19.6 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0)
Platelets 245 x10^9/L (150 to 400)
INR 1.0 (0.9 to 1.2)
C-reactive protein 210 mg/L (less than 5)
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.explanation: This man has fever, a headache that built up over hours, photophobia and neck stiffness, so he has bacterial meningitis until proven otherwise. The right first steps have been taken: blood cultures, then dexamethasone and ceftriaxone without waiting for any test. Lumbar puncture is the next investigation. CSF cell count, protein, glucose ratio, Gram stain, culture with susceptibilities and PCR confirm the diagnosis, identify the organism and guide how antibiotics are narrowed and how long they are given. Under eTG, CT before LP is needed only if there is a contraindication: reduced or falling GCS, focal neurological signs, a recent seizure, papilloedema or immunocompromise. He has none of these. His platelets and INR are normal, so it is safe to go straight to LP. Organisms can often still be found in CSF in the first hours after antibiotics, and cell count, protein and glucose changes last longer, so LP should be done promptly and not put off.
why: Correct: with GCS 15, no focal signs, no seizure, no papilloedema and normal platelets and coagulation, LP is safe without imaging, and CSF analysis is the test that confirms bacterial meningitis and identifies the organism.

He drinks two standard drinks a week and eats a mixed diet. His blood pressure is 134/82 mm Hg and pulse is 76/min. Pinprick and 10 g monofilament sensation are reduced symmetrically to the mid-shins. Vibration sense is absent at both great toes. Ankle reflexes are absent, knee reflexes are normal and plantar responses are flexor. Power and tone are normal. Romberg test is positive. Pedal pulses are palpable. Investigations: HbA1c 8.4% (target 7.0% or less), haemoglobin 141 g/L, MCV 92 fL (80 to 100), eGFR 74 mL/min/1.73 m2 and TSH 2.1 mIU/L (0.5 to 4.0).
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Nerve conduction studies of the legs
questions.explanation: This man has a typical distal symmetrical sensorimotor polyneuropathy. The loss is length-dependent and stocking-shaped, he has lost protective sensation and vibration sense, his ankle reflexes are absent while his knee reflexes are kept, and he has sensory ataxia. This fits poorly controlled type 2 diabetes. Before calling it diabetic neuropathy, the treatable mimics need to be excluded. His TSH and eGFR are normal and he drinks little, so the main mimic left is vitamin B12 deficiency. Metformin reduces B12 absorption, and he has taken it for 8 years. A normal MCV does not exclude B12 deficiency, because neuropathy can come before anaemia or macrocytosis. Australian guidance (eTG Diabetes and the RACGP type 2 diabetes handbook) recommends checking B12 in people on long-term metformin, especially when neuropathy appears. Diabetic neuropathy is a clinical diagnosis, so nerve conduction studies, imaging, CSF analysis and biopsy are only needed for atypical features. These include asymmetry, rapid progression, marked weakness, early involvement of the hands, or upper motor neuron or sphincter signs.
why: Wrong: nerve conduction studies are kept for atypical features, such as asymmetry, rapid progression or prominent weakness, and they would not separate diabetic from B12-related neuropathy.
Wrong: he has no back pain, sphincter symptoms, saddle anaesthesia, upper motor neuron signs or dermatomal pattern, so imaging the spine is not indicated.

Wrong: CSF protein is used when chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy is suspected, which presents with proximal and distal weakness and loss of all reflexes, not a purely distal sensory picture.
Wrong: nerve biopsy is invasive and is kept for suspected vasculitic or infiltrative neuropathy, which would present with asymmetric or rapidly progressive deficits.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 18 hours of constant right upper quadrant pain that began after a takeaway dinner. The pain radiates to her right shoulder, and she has vomited four times. She has had three shorter, similar episodes over the past 6 months. She takes a combined oral contraceptive pill and drinks alcohol occasionally. Her temperature is 38.4 °C, pulse 104/min, blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg and respiratory rate 18/min. She is not jaundiced and is alert. Her right upper quadrant is tender, and Murphy's sign is positive. Blood tests show: white cell count 14.9 x10^9/L (4.0–11.0), CRP 128 mg/L (<5), total bilirubin 15 µmol/L (<20), ALP 131 U/L (30–110), GGT 52 U/L (<38), ALT 44 U/L (<35), lipase 40 U/L (<60) and serum beta-hCG <2 IU/L. Ultrasound shows multiple gallstones, a gallbladder wall of 7 mm with pericholecystic fluid, and a common bile duct of 4 mm with no duct stone seen.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of her liver function results?
options: Biliary obstruction, warranting urgent ERCP to clear the duct
Reactive cholestatic change, making choledocholithiasis unlikely
Hepatocellular injury, suggesting a superimposed acute viral hepatitis
Early cholangitis, warranting urgent biliary decompression
Alcohol-related injury, suggested by the elevated GGT level
questions.explanation: She has acute calculous cholecystitis. She has constant right upper quadrant pain for more than a few hours, fever, a positive Murphy's sign, a raised white cell count and CRP, and an ultrasound showing gallstones, a thickened wall and pericholecystic fluid. Her ALP, GGT and ALT are all less than 1.5 times the upper limit of normal. Her bilirubin is normal and her common bile duct is not dilated (4 mm) with no duct stone seen. Small rises in ALP, GGT and ALT are common in cholecystitis. Inflammation next to the liver and the bile ducts causes them, not a blocked common bile duct. With a normal bilirubin, a normal duct calibre and no stone seen, her risk of a common bile duct stone is low. She does not need a preoperative MRCP or ERCP and can go to early laparoscopic cholecystectomy, with IV antibiotics as eTG recommends. A raised bilirubin, a dilated duct or a duct stone would change this. With fever, they would point to cholangitis. Option A is wrong because a blocked duct would normally raise the bilirubin and widen the duct, and she has neither. Option B is wrong because the transaminases are barely raised and the pattern is mildly cholestatic, not the large ALT rise of acute hepatitis. Option D is wrong because cholangitis needs signs of a blocked duct (jaundice or a raised bilirubin, a dilated duct) as well as fever, and she has none. Option E is wrong because a small GGT rise alongside a raised ALP fits reactive cholestasis, and she rarely drinks.
why: A blocked common bile duct would normally raise the bilirubin and dilate the duct, but her bilirubin is 15 µmol/L and her duct is 4 mm, so ERCP is not indicated.
Acute viral hepatitis causes a large ALT rise, often in the hundreds or thousands, but her ALT is only 44 U/L with a mildly cholestatic pattern, and the ultrasound explains her symptoms.
Cholangitis needs fever plus evidence of a blocked duct, such as jaundice, a raised bilirubin or a dilated duct, and she has none of these, so urgent decompression is not needed.
A small GGT rise alongside a raised ALP fits reactive cholestasis, and she rarely drinks, so alcohol does not explain these results.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman, a primary school teacher, comes to the rheumatology outpatient clinic to discuss treatment of rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed 2 weeks ago. She has had 4 months of pain and swelling in both hands, wrists and forefeet, with 2 hours of morning stiffness. She has a 3-year-old daughter. She stopped her combined oral contraceptive pill 2 months ago, is trying to conceive and does not want to use contraception or delay pregnancy. Her only medicine is naproxen 500 mg twice daily. Temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse 78/min and blood pressure 116/72 mm Hg. She has soft synovial swelling of both wrists and the 2nd to 4th MCP and PIP joints, and the DIP joints are spared. CRP is 31 mg/L (reference below 5), rheumatoid factor 88 IU/mL (below 20) and anti-CCP 240 U/mL (below 7). Hepatitis B and C serology is negative, ALT is 22 U/L, eGFR is above 90 mL/min/1.73 m² and urine beta-hCG is negative. A hand X-ray shows periarticular osteopenia and a marginal erosion at the right 2nd MCP joint.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate disease-modifying drug to start?
questions.explanation: She has early, seropositive, erosive rheumatoid arthritis with poor prognostic features, so she needs a DMARD started now to prevent more joint damage. The most important risk in her case is the drug harming a pregnancy, because she is trying to conceive and will not use contraception. Under eTG and Australian Rheumatology Association guidance, sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine are the conventional synthetic DMARDs that can be used before conception and through pregnancy. Sulfasalazine is started at a low dose and increased to 1 g twice daily. It is a folate antagonist, so she should also take high-dose folic acid (5 mg daily) before conception. It can be combined with hydroxychloroquine and short-term low-dose prednisolone if needed. She should plan her pregnancy with the rheumatologist and stop naproxen while trying to conceive. Leflunomide and methotrexate are teratogenic and need reliable contraception. Mycophenolate and tofacitinib are also unsuitable.
why: Leflunomide is teratogenic and its active metabolite stays in the body for up to 2 years, so a woman trying to conceive would need a washout with cholestyramine; it is contraindicated for her.

Methotrexate is usually the first-line DMARD, but it is teratogenic and abortifacient, so it needs reliable contraception and must be stopped before conception; it is contraindicated while she is actively trying to conceive.
Mycophenolate is a strong teratogen that causes miscarriage and malformations, and it is not a standard DMARD for rheumatoid arthritis.
Tofacitinib is a JAK inhibitor that should be avoided around conception and in pregnancy, and in Australia it is reserved for disease that has not responded to conventional synthetic DMARDs.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman sees her general practitioner with 3 months of palpitations, heat intolerance and 6 kg of unintentional weight loss. She is not breathless and has no chest pain. She has no past medical history, takes no medicines or supplements, and has a contraceptive implant. Temperature is 37.0 °C, pulse 110/min and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 126/78 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16/min and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. She is alert and has a fine tremor, warm moist hands, and bilateral lid retraction and mild proptosis, with normal visual acuity, colour vision and eye movements. There is a diffuse, smooth, non-tender goitre with a bruit. There are no signs of heart failure. ECG shows atrial fibrillation at 110/min with narrow QRS complexes. TSH is <0.01 mIU/L (0.4–4.0), free T4 48 pmol/L (10–20), free T3 18.5 pmol/L (3.5–6.5) and TSH receptor antibodies 12.4 IU/L (<1.8). questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: She has Graves' disease, shown by suppressed TSH, high free T4 and T3, strongly positive TRAb, a diffuse goitre with a bruit and orbitopathy. It is complicated by thyrotoxic atrial fibrillation. She is haemodynamically stable, afebrile and alert, with no heart failure, so she does not have thyroid storm and can be managed as an outpatient. eTG recommends a non-selective beta blocker such as propranolol to control the heart rate and adrenergic symptoms. It also recommends a thionamide, with carbimazole first-line outside the first trimester, to make her euthyroid. Baseline FBC and LFTs are normal and she is not pregnant. Thyrotoxic AF usually reverts to sinus rhythm once she is euthyroid. Her CHA2DS2-VA score is 0, so anticoagulation is not indicated. She must be told to stop carbimazole and have a same-day FBC if she gets a sore throat, fever or mouth ulcers. Amiodarone is wrong because its iodine load worsens thyrotoxicosis, and she does not need anticoagulation. Digoxin works poorly in a hyperadrenergic state, and propylthiouracil is kept for the first trimester or thyroid storm because it can damage the liver. Radioiodine is not first-line here and can worsen her active orbitopathy. Cardioversion while she is still thyrotoxic usually fails, so it is deferred until she is euthyroid.
why: Amiodarone's iodine load can worsen thyrotoxicosis, and with a CHA2DS2-VA score of 0 she does not need anticoagulation.
Digoxin controls the rate poorly in a hyperadrenergic thyrotoxic state, and propylthiouracil is kept for the first trimester of pregnancy or thyroid storm because it can cause severe liver injury.
Radioiodine is not first-line treatment for a new, uncontrolled presentation and can worsen her active Graves' orbitopathy, especially before she is euthyroid.
Cardioversion in a patient who is still thyrotoxic often fails and the AF tends to come back, so it is deferred until she is euthyroid, by which time the AF usually reverts on its own.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman presents to a metropolitan emergency department with 10 days of worsening breathlessness. It has been severe since overnight, and she has orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea. Six weeks ago she had an anterior myocardial infarction treated with a stent. Since then she has been taking over-the-counter naproxen for knee pain. Her pulse is 110/min and regular, blood pressure 194/102 mm Hg, respiratory rate 30/min and SpO2 87% on room air. She has a raised jugular venous pressure, a third heart sound and bilateral basal crackles. Her ECG shows sinus tachycardia with anterior Q waves, unchanged from her discharge ECG. Her chest X-ray shows bilateral perihilar opacification and small effusions. NT-proBNP is 7900 ng/L (age-adjusted rule-in level above 900 ng/L). High-sensitivity troponin I is 38 ng/L, then 37 ng/L at 3 hours (female 99th percentile 16 ng/L). Creatinine is 142 µmol/L. After CPAP, glyceryl trinitrate and intravenous furosemide, she is comfortable on 2 L/min of oxygen by nasal prongs.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.explanation: This woman has acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. She has orthopnoea, PND, a raised JVP, an S3, crackles, alveolar oedema with effusions on X-ray and a very high NT-proBNP. The likely cause is ischaemic left ventricular dysfunction after her recent anterior MI, made worse by NSAID-related fluid retention and hypertension. Her two troponin values are stable and barely raised, and her ECG has not changed, so this is chronic myocardial injury rather than a new infarct. The 2018 National Heart Foundation and CSANZ heart failure guideline recommends transthoracic echocardiography for every patient with suspected heart failure. Echo confirms the diagnosis and measures the LVEF, which decides between HFrEF and HFpEF and therefore which survival-improving treatments she should get. Echo also looks for mechanical complications of the recent MI (mitral regurgitation, ventricular septal defect, aneurysm, left ventricular thrombus), regional wall motion problems and valve disease. It is quick, done at the bedside and needs no contrast or radiation.
why: Incorrect: orthopnoea, PND, an S3, alveolar oedema and an NT-proBNP of 7900 explain her hypoxia, so pulmonary embolism is unlikely and iodinated contrast with a creatinine of 142 µmol/L brings risk for no gain.
Incorrect: her troponin is flat with no new ECG change, so there is no acute coronary syndrome needing urgent angiography, and the contrast load would add to her kidney injury.
Incorrect: cardiac MRI is a second-line test for when echo images are poor or the cause is unclear, not the first test for ventricular function in an acutely unwell patient.
Incorrect: a V/Q scan tests for pulmonary embolism, which the clinical picture does not suggest, and alveolar oedema and effusions make the scan hard to interpret.

questions.explanation: Quantify breathlessness against the patient's baseline (distance, stairs or activities) and ask specifically about orthopnoea (number of pillows), PND and ankle swelling.
why: No chest pain, a gradual 4-month course, a flat troponin (24 then 25) and an ECG unchanged from 12 months ago.
No weight loss, haemoptysis or hoarseness, and no mass or nodule on CXR.
No cough, sputum or wheeze, orthopnoea and PND with oedema, and no hyperinflation on CXR.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man in general practice. Eight years of type 2 diabetes with HbA1c 8.9% from metformin non-adherence, gradual symmetrical stocking sensory loss to mid-shin, absent ankle reflexes, positive Romberg and loss of protective sensation.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Spinal cord or cauda equina compression
questions.explanation: Glove-and-stocking sensory loss points to a length-dependent peripheral neuropathy, a dermatomal pattern to a root or cord lesion, and a single nerve territory to a nerve compression or injury.
why: Against cord compression: no upper motor neuron signs (flexor plantars, no clonus, normal tone, knee reflexes not brisk) and no sensory level; against cauda equina: no back pain, no sphincter or saddle symptoms, and a gradual symmetrical stocking pattern rather than a saddle or radicular one.
He rarely takes the metformin, he is not vegetarian or vegan, and his B12, folate and MCV are normal.
He drinks only an occasional can of beer on weekends, and his GGT, LFTs and MCV are normal.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man in the emergency department. Five months of progressive breathlessness with 20 kg weight loss, night sweats, blood-tinged sputum, a hoarse voice, clubbing, a hard right supraclavicular node and 50 pack-years, with a large unilateral right effusion on X-ray.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: In a smoker with progressive breathlessness, ask directly about weight loss, haemoptysis, hoarseness and night sweats, and quantify smoking in pack-years (20 a day for 50 years is 50 pack-years).
why: The 5-month gradual course, no pleuritic pain or sick contacts, and a normal white cell count.
Haemoptysis, a hoarse voice and a supraclavicular node point more to a primary lung cancer.
Born in Australia with no TB travel, contacts or past TB, and the smoking history and node make cancer more likely.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman in the emergency department. Three weeks of constant burning forefoot pain that is worse lying flat and eased by hanging the leg, after years of claudication, with gangrene of three toes, absent right popliteal and pedal pulses, right ABI 0.28 and heavy cardiovascular risk.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia of the right leg
questions.explanation: Ischaemic rest pain is constant forefoot and toe pain, worse lying flat or at night and eased by hanging the leg down. Present for more than 2 weeks, or with gangrene or an ulcer, it defines chronic limb-threatening ischaemia.
why: She has no new numbness or weakness, power is 5/5 and her rhythm is regular, with a stable 3-week course.
Her calves are soft, non-tender and equal with no warmth or swelling, and the pain is in the toes and eased by dependency.
The current pain is constant at rest and there is tissue loss, so she has moved beyond claudication.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man on the ward. Day 5 after major orthopaedic surgery with little mobilisation, sudden pleuritic chest pain, breathlessness, HR 124, SpO2 92%, a swollen red right calf, Wells 9, and bilateral lower lobe emboli on CTPA.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness after major orthopaedic surgery is PE until proven otherwise: always examine both legs for a DVT.
why: Sharp right-sided pleuritic pain without radiation, sweating or nausea, no ischaemic change on the ECG, and two normal troponins.
Pain is not tearing and does not go to the back, BP is equal in both arms, and the aorta is normal on CT.
No cough or sputum, a clear chest on examination and no consolidation on CT.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man in the emergency department. Breathlessness and sharp left pleuritic pain straight after a fall onto the left side, with tracheal deviation to the right, distended neck veins, left hyper-resonance and reduced breath sounds, tachycardia, hypotension, hypoxia, and complete left lung collapse with mediastinal shift on X-ray.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis: breathlessness, hypoxia, tachycardia, hypotension, distended neck veins, tracheal deviation away from the affected side, and hyper-resonance with reduced or absent breath sounds. Decompress before imaging.
why: Heart sounds are not muffled, the trachea is deviated, and the left chest is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds on one side; a normal cardiac silhouette does not exclude acute tamponade, so eFAST is still needed.
The left chest is hyper-resonant rather than dull, the X-ray shows no effusion or fluid level, the neck veins are distended rather than flat, and the Hb is normal.
No leg swelling, immobility, travel or previous clots, and the trauma and one-sided signs explain the picture.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy in the emergency department. Acute expiratory wheeze with recession over a few hours after a 2-day cold, a partial response to salbutamol, rhinovirus on PCR, smoke exposure, day-care, preterm birth and atopy.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: In a wheezy preschool child, always ask about anaphylaxis (skin signs with another system involved, new foods, stings) and an inhaled foreign body (sudden choking), because both need different, urgent treatment.
why: There was no choking episode, the wheeze is bilateral and symmetrical, and it followed a coryzal illness.
No urticaria, angioedema, vomiting or floppiness, no new food or sting, and the onset was gradual after a cold.
He has no wheeze or night cough between colds and no other triggers, and at 3 years episodic viral wheeze is more likely.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old man in the emergency department. Two weeks of worsening breathlessness with orthopnoea, PND and pink frothy sputum a month after an MI, 2 weeks of regular ibuprofen, a raised JVP, S3 and crackles, NT-proBNP 8400 and a chest X-ray showing alveolar oedema, upper lobe diversion and effusions.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Ask every breathless patient about orthopnoea (how many pillows), PND, frothy pink sputum and exercise tolerance, and examine the JVP, heart sounds for an S3, lung bases and ankles.
why: No chest pain, nausea or radiation, and the ECG is unchanged from his discharge ECG.
No pleuritic pain, calf swelling or immobility, and orthopnoea, PND, an S3 and oedema on X-ray explain the picture.
No fever or purulent sputum, normal WCC, only a small CRP rise, and the change is bilateral with upper lobe diversion and effusions.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman in the emergency department. Constant right upper quadrant pain for over 24 hours after a fatty meal, with right shoulder radiation, fever to 38.9, a positive Murphy's sign, WCC 14.2, CRP 96, and an ultrasound showing a 5 mm wall, pericholecystic fluid and a stone impacted in the gallbladder neck.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute coronary syndrome or right lower lobe pneumonia
questions.explanation: Biliary colic is postprandial pain that settles within about 6 hours. Constant RUQ pain for hours, with fever, Murphy's sign and raised WCC and CRP, is acute cholecystitis.
why: No clinical jaundice, bilirubin only 26, common bile duct 5 mm with no intrahepatic dilatation, and normal BP and lactate.
No chest pain, breathlessness or cough, chest clear including the right base, SpO2 97% on room air, and the ECG shows sinus tachycardia with no ST or T wave changes.
This pain has been constant and worsening for over a day, with fever, raised WCC and CRP, and a thickened gallbladder wall.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man in the emergency department. He shared needles 2 months ago, had a prodrome of fever, arthralgia, urticaria and malaise, now has jaundice with dark urine and pale stools and a tender smooth liver, with ALT 1635 and HBsAg, IgM anti-HBc and HBeAg positive.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Paracetamol or other drug-induced liver injury
questions.explanation: Viral hepatitis has a prodrome (anorexia, malaise, fever, RUQ pain; urticaria and arthralgia especially in hepatitis B), then an icteric phase with dark urine, pale stools, itch and jaundice.
why: No rigors, haemodynamically stable, normal WCC with only a mild CRP rise, transaminase rise far greater than the ALP rise, a viral prodrome, and no duct dilatation or stones on ultrasound.
He denies any paracetamol, overdose, other medicines or supplements, and the paracetamol level is undetectable.
The HCV antibody is negative, although this can be falsely reassuring in the window period, and the hepatitis B serology already explains the illness.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman in general practice. Returned from Thailand a month ago after eating street food without pre-travel vaccination, with a 2-week prodrome, then jaundice, a hepatocellular picture and a positive HAV IgM.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Dark urine and pale stools mean conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Always ask the 4 Ps (pee, poo, pruritus, pain) in jaundice.
why: No gallstones or bile duct dilatation on ultrasound, ALT far higher than ALP, and a normal white cell count.
Normal haemoglobin and platelets, and a positive HAV IgM explains the picture.
Constant pain not related to food, no history of gallstones, and no stones or duct dilatation on ultrasound.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman in the emergency department. RUQ pain, fever with rigors and jaundice (Charcot's triad), pale stools, dark urine and itch, cholestatic LFTs with WCC 17.8 and CRP 186, and an 11 mm common bile duct with a distal stone.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: RUQ pain, fever with rigors and jaundice (Charcot's triad) is acute cholangitis until proven otherwise. Confusion and hypotension (Reynolds' pentad) mean severe disease.
why: Lipase 42 is normal, the pain does not go through to the back, and the visualised pancreas is normal.
She is jaundiced with obstructive features, Murphy's sign is negative, and the gallbladder wall is thin with no pericholecystic fluid.
No IV drugs, travel or unsafe sex, the LFTs are cholestatic with ALP and GGT raised more than ALT, and the bile ducts are dilated.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man in the emergency department. Two days of worsening headache with fever, vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia and positive Kernig's sign in a man on prednisolone, with turbid neutrophilic CSF, high protein and a low glucose ratio.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fever, headache, neck stiffness and photophobia mean meningitis until proven otherwise. Always ask about and look for a non-blanching rash.
why: He is oriented with GCS 15, intact attention, no drowsiness, behaviour change, seizures or focal signs.
It was not a thunderclap or worst-ever, with no collapse, and has built over 2 days with fever; the CT is normal and the CSF has minimal red cells.
His CSF is turbid with neutrophils, a high protein and a low glucose, and he has a CRP of 214 with a raised lactate.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old woman in general practice. Fever of 39 °C, a worsening generalised headache, neck stiffness, photophobia and a positive Kernig's sign in an 18-year-old after a crowded festival with a shared tent and uncertain meningococcal vaccination; the CSF is neutrophilic with a low glucose, Gram-negative diplococci and a positive N. meningitidis PCR.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fever, headache, neck stiffness and photophobia mean bacterial meningitis until proven otherwise. Ask about and look for a rash, but its absence does not exclude meningococcal disease.
why: She is alert and oriented (GCS 15) with no seizures, behaviour change or focal signs, and the CSF is neutrophilic with organisms seen.
The headache built up over hours, she has a fever and a coryzal prodrome, and the CSF has no xanthochromia and only 5 red cells.
The CSF has 8500 neutrophils, a protein of 1.1 g/L, a glucose ratio of 0.24 and Gram-negative diplococci.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman in general practice. Five stereotyped attacks of severe, one-sided throbbing headache lasting 6 to 7 hours, with light and noise sensitivity and nausea, each preceded by about 20 minutes of fully reversible visual aura, with a normal examination.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Ask how fast the headache started and whether it matches previous attacks. A gradual, stereotyped headache with a normal examination and no red flags (SNOOP) needs no imaging.
why: The onset was gradual, it is the same as four previous attacks, and the neurological examination and fundi are normal.
She is afebrile, with no neck stiffness, negative Kernig's sign and no rash.
The visual symptoms are positive (dots, jumbled lines), spread gradually, resolve fully and are followed by headache, with no weakness, numbness or speech change and a normal examination.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man in general practice. Two months of bloody, mucousy diarrhoea with LIF pain, weight loss, fatigue and erythema nodosum, and continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum to 25 cm with crypt distortion.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chronic bloody, mucousy diarrhoea with weight loss in a young adult is inflammatory bowel disease until proven otherwise; IBS cannot be diagnosed with blood, weight loss, nocturnal stools or a raised calprotectin.
why: Age 25, and colonoscopy found no mass, with no dysplasia on biopsy.
Continuous inflammation from the rectum, normal terminal ileum, inflammation confined to the mucosa, no granulomas and no perianal disease.
No travel, sick contacts or antibiotics, a 2-month course, and negative stool PCR, culture, C. difficile and parasite tests.
